For Azerbaijan, therefore, the main question is not so much whether to join the agreement, but how to benefit from closer ties among its existing partners – Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Israel – without taking on formal commitments. This is precisely the flexibility that its multi-vector policy provides.

Mecca defence agreement and Azerbaijan

World.title: Number of Iranian companies in Georgia up 510% since 2012 – EPRC
World.content:
Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

According to data from the Economic Policy Research Center (EPRC), the number of Iranian companies in Georgia has increased by around 510% since 2012, exceeding 12,800 by 2025–26.

EPRC says the figures are based on data from Geostat and the National Bank of Georgia. The organisation also notes that despite the sharp rise in the number of companies, foreign direct investment from Iran into Georgia has remained relatively low in recent years.

“Between 2013 and 2024, Iranian investment totalled $41 million. Although this is more than in the previous period, the amount per company remains quite small,” EPRC said.

According to the organisation, net foreign direct investment from Iran stood at -$0.65 million in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2025 put the figure at around $0.4 million.

EPRC estimates that Iran’s share of total foreign direct investment in Georgia remains small, according to official statistics.

The centre says Iranian companies registered in Georgia are mainly involved in small-scale trade, real estate transactions, services, construction, logistics and re-export.

“Most of this activity involves small and medium-sized businesses and is less connected to large-scale manufacturing, industrial or technology projects,” EPRC said.

The organisation notes that the activities of these companies have not led to significant job creation. It also says that dozens of companies are often registered at the same address.

According to EPRC, tourism has seen the most notable growth in economic activity linked to Iran. Between 2022 and 2024, tourism revenues from Iran rose from $91.1 million to $151.1 million, an increase of 65%. However, tourism revenues fell by 17.8% in 2025.

Why the number of Iranian companies is growing much faster than investment

The centre believes that the rapid increase in the number of companies, alongside relatively low levels of investment and official financial flows, raises questions about the true scale of their activities.

“Why is the number of Iranian companies growing much faster than investment and official financial inflows overall?” EPRC asks.

The organisation says that, given that a significant part of Iran’s financial sector operates under international sanctions, economic transactions may be taking place through alternative and potentially less transparent financial channels.

EPRC notes that if some economic activity takes place outside the traditional banking system or with limited transparency, this makes it harder for the state to effectively monitor financial flows. It also increases the risks of sanctions evasion and money laundering.

The centre also points to international practice, where such models are sometimes associated with nominal or so-called “paper” companies. These companies are officially registered, but their actual economic activity may be very limited.

According to EPRC, such companies are sometimes used for re-export operations, intermediary financial transactions, or to circumvent sanctions and regulatory requirements in different countries.

“When the number of companies grows rapidly but this is not accompanied by a corresponding increase in investment, production, exports or employment, questions arise about the real economic significance of their activities,” the organisation said.

EPRC also points to the visa-free regime between Georgia and the EU, saying that this could make the country more attractive to Iranian citizens and businesses.

According to the centre, the US sanctions imposed on Shelbit, a cryptocurrency company registered in Georgia and owned by an Iranian citizen, highlight the range of possible ways to circumvent sanctions.

EPRC believes that, in light of this case and the sharp increase in the number of companies opened in Georgia by Iranian citizens, the current figures should be viewed with additional risks in mind.

Growth in the number of Iranian companies in Georgia

World.title: Tbilisi’s new zoo ready to welcome visitors – video
World.content:
The new Tbilisi Zoo will open to visitors in August 2026. Construction began after the 2015 floods, and the zoo is opening in stages. Although work is still under way, visitors will soon be able to explore the new site.

One of Tbilisi Zoo’s best-known residents, Shani the lion cub, has already moved to the new zoo.

___________________________________________

___________________________________________

As David Taktakishvili, deputy director of Tbilisi Zoo, explains, the new zoo covers a large area, and the site is being developed in stages. Some animals have already been moved, but construction of the enclosures is still under way. Construction and infrastructure work will therefore continue after the zoo opens.

The zoo administration believes the public should already have the opportunity to see for themselves how a new-generation zoo is taking shape and how much better the animals will live in their new environment.

When the new zoo opens to visitors, the Caucasus biogeographical zone will be accessible to the public. In the future, the zoo will bring together spaces representing different regions of the world. At the first stage, however, the focus will be on the local flora and fauna of the Caucasus. Visitors will see red deer, bison, bears, wolves and other local species in this zone.

Construction of the African zone is currently under way. The new zoo will gradually add other biogeographical zones in the future.

In recent years, the role of zoos has also changed significantly. Today, one of their main functions is nature conservation, including protecting, breeding and caring for endangered species. The new, modern facility will serve this purpose and, in the future, will become not only a place for visitors but also an important wildlife conservation centre.

Admission prices will remain unchanged: free for children under three, 2 lari ($0.76) for children aged three to 12, and 4 lari ($1.53) for visitors aged 12 and over.

Some animals will remain at the old zoo, which will continue to operate as usual.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

New Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgian opposition figure investigated for ‘treason’ over comments on Abkhazia war
World.content:
Giorgi Baramidze case

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has opened an investigation into comments by Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, about the war in Abkhazia. The case concerns charges of treason and actions that threaten state interests. The investigation focuses on his account of how prisoners of war were treated during the early stages of the conflict. Baramidze made the comments on a podcast, triggering a political backlash. The de facto authorities in Abkhazia have also reacted to his remarks.

What did Baramidze say?

Giorgi Baramidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, discussed the war in Abkhazia on Yago Khvichia’s “Birth of Georgia” programme.

Speaking about the exchange of prisoners, he said:

“We did not take prisoners, we had no prisoners, we executed them.”

The remark prompted a strong reaction from government officials. Baramidze later clarified several times what he meant.

He said he was referring to the early stages of the war, when the Georgian side did not yet have a regular and organised army. Baramidze later explained that people enraged by the deaths of their relatives in the fighting did not take enemy fighters prisoner.

“At first, the situation was as follows: people who were enraged after their mothers, fathers and relatives had been killed did not take prisoners during the fighting but killed them instead. That is the bitter truth about the early stages of the war. I know this because I personally took part in prisoner exchanges,” Baramidze said.

According to him, the situation later changed. The Georgian side began taking prisoners, which made exchanges possible. Baramidze said that around 200 Georgian prisoners were eventually brought home as a result.

“My deputy and I could not have exchanged 200 Georgian prisoners if our side had not taken any prisoners at all,” he added.

Baramidze also denies that his comments were directed against the Georgian army or the state as a whole. He insists that he was referring specifically to the situation during the early stages of the war.

At the same time, he stressed Russia’s responsibility, saying that the Russian Federation acted as an aggressor and occupier in the wars of 1992–93 and 2008.

Why has the prosecutor’s office opened an investigation?

Georgia’s Prosecutor General’s Office opened the investigation at the request of the State Service of Veterans Affairs.

According to the agency, prosecutors are investigating the case under Articles 307¹ and 318 of the Criminal Code. The first concerns treason, while the second covers actions that threaten Georgia’s state interests.

The prosecutor’s office said:

“The investigation began following an appeal from the State Service of Veterans Affairs concerning comments made by Giorgi Baramidze, a member of the United National Movement. The case concerns his remarks about the war in Abkhazia and the prisoner exchange process, which he made on Yago Khvichia’s programme ‘Birth of Georgia’.”

As part of the investigation, prosecutors also summoned Koba Kobaladze, head of the State Service of Veterans Affairs, for questioning.

Baramidze sees the investigation as political persecution.

“The prosecutor’s office has opened a case against me for ‘betraying Georgia’! I am not afraid of your persecution, let alone your dirty propaganda!” he wrote on social media.

What does the government say?

Members of the Georgian Dream party do not consider Baramidze’s remarks simply an unfortunate choice of words. They argue that such statements could harm Georgia’s national interests and international standing.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described Baramidze’s comments as morally unacceptable. As for the legal assessment, he said the relevant authorities should make that decision.

“As for the legal aspect, the relevant authorities will determine that, but from a moral standpoint, what this man said is simply disgusting,” Kobakhidze said.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili linked Baramidze’s remarks to a broader political context. He said the opposition had previously promoted what he called a harmful narrative about Georgia’s 2008 war, and that the same was now happening with the war in Abkhazia.

Alexander Tabatadze, chairman of the parliamentary Defence and Security Committee, said Baramidze’s comments could damage Georgia’s international standing.

He argued that such remarks could be used against Georgia. Tabatadze also said the wording insulted veterans of the Abkhazia war and those who were killed in the fighting.

The opposition also criticises the remarks

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said Baramidze’s comments were inaccurate. However, he argued that an incorrect statement did not amount to treason.

“What was said is not true… I don’t know where this story came from. In my view, the words got ahead of the meaning, and that is not good. But treason and a crime are different things, and this is not how they are committed,” Gvaramia said.

He said he had no doubts about Baramidze’s patriotism. He described the prosecutor’s investigation as political persecution.

Shalva Kereselidze, a representative of Gakharia for Georgia, called Baramidze’s remarks politically inappropriate and unworthy of a statesman.

“This is a statement unworthy of a statesman, and it is inappropriate both politically and from a human standpoint,” Kereselidze said.

The United National Movement, meanwhile, says the investigation is entirely politically motivated. The party also pointed out that Baramidze fought in the wars in Abkhazia and Ukraine.

“While the Kremlin regards Giorgi Baramidze as an enemy and persecutes him, the Georgian Dream government is accusing the same person of treason,” the party said in a statement.

Expert: “Baramidze’s account does not match the facts”

Conflict expert and former state minister Paata Zakareishvili has questioned the factual accuracy of Baramidze’s account.

Zakareishvili himself worked on prisoner exchanges during the Abkhazia war. He said Baramidze’s account differed so sharply from the realities of the time that he initially thought Baramidze was referring to a different war.

He also disputed Baramidze’s claim that he took part in the work of the prisoner exchange commission.

“Baramidze mentions this commission, but to be honest, he did not take part in its work,” Zakareishvili said.

He noted that documents exist detailing the commission’s work, but Baramidze’s name does not appear in them.

At the same time, Zakareishvili questioned the legal grounds for the investigation. In his view, false or exaggerated statements should not provide grounds for criminal prosecution.

“I still believe that Baramidze does not deserve punishment. I will do everything I can to prove that he was not a member of the commission. His comments are simply speculation, nothing more,” Zakareishvili said.

He also said he was ready to provide the prosecutor’s office with the information he has.

How the case moved beyond the domestic political conflict

The de facto Abkhaz foreign ministry has already responded to Baramidze’s remarks.

The ministry used his comments to reinforce its own historical narrative about the conflict. Its statement described the 1992–93 war as Georgia’s armed aggression against Abkhazia.

Sukhumi also criticised the investigation into Baramidze.

“It is clear that this criminal prosecution should serve as a warning to anyone prepared to speak openly about Georgia’s armed aggression and the crimes committed during it,” the statement said.

Giorgi Baramidze case

World.title: ‘Regional stability is main achievement’: assessing Washington peace summit one year on
World.content:
Washington peace summit: one year on

“The peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan is visible and tangible to everyone,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in a statement marking the events of 8 August.

A year ago, on this day, Washington hosted a historic peace summit, with US President Donald Trump acting as mediator. Yerevan and Baku initialled a peace agreement, signed a declaration on the TRIPP project – a transit route through Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan (the “Trump Route”) – and signed a number of bilateral documents with the United States.

Pashinyan said the peace agreement “awaits signing and ratification”. He added that practical work on TRIPP would begin in the near future and become a “major regional and international event”.

The prime minister congratulated the people of Armenia and Azerbaijan on the landmark date of 8 August.

“Finally, we have a day that brings peace rather than stirs up our emotions,” he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also issued a statement, highlighting the “courage and foresight” shown by both countries over the past year.

“We look forward to further progress towards lasting and durable peace in the South Caucasus,” the secretary of state said.

Pashinyan held phone calls with Donald Trump and Ilham Aliyev.

Armenian analysts said the main outcome of the Washington summit was the establishment of stability in the region.

They noted positive developments despite what they described as Baku’s “aggressive agenda”, including its calls for Azerbaijanis to return to what it calls “Western Azerbaijan”. The term refers to almost the entire sovereign territory of Armenia.

Pashinyan on unresolved issues and how to make “peace irreversible”

In his address to the nation, Pashinyan once again said that peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan had been established.

“But this, of course, does not mean that we have already reached the end of the road in implementing the peace agenda,” he added.

According to the prime minister, the following issues remain unresolved:

signing and ratifying the peace agreement,

delimiting the Armenian-Azerbaijani border,

“the continued detention of our compatriots in Azerbaijan” [referring to 19 Armenian prisoners held in Baku].

He also said that 8 August 2025 had marked a turning point, dividing Armenia’s history into the periods “before and after this date”. Pashinyan described the period before 8 August as a dead end, while the period since then has offered “limitless opportunities”.

Pashinyan said the main political and social-psychological result of the Washington summit was that “the wheel of our history has once again fallen into our hands”.

He identified the implementation of the “Trump Route” project as another major outcome:

“It will not only end Armenia’s blockade in the very near future and become the backbone of Armenia’s and the region’s economy, but will also help Armenia and Azerbaijan start seeing each other not as an obstacle, but as a route and as a neighbour.”

The transit route was named the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” after the mediator, as the Armenian and Azerbaijani authorities had been unable to reach an agreement on the issue for several years.

Pashinyan also outlined steps that Armenia and Azerbaijan should take to make the peace between them irreversible:

“We need to put an end to discussions about the ‘right of Armenians to return to Nagorno-Karabakh’ and the ‘return of Armenian refugees from Azerbaijan’. Azerbaijan, for its part, needs to end discussions about ‘Western Azerbaijan’ and the ‘right of Western Azerbaijanis to return’. This is an issue that both Armenia and Azerbaijan must resolve in the name of our generations’ right to live together in peace.”

“We hope to see further progress”, Rubio says

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that over the past 12 months, the United States had continued to work with Armenia and Azerbaijan. He highlighted the importance of the TRIPP project. According to Rubio, the transit route is gradually becoming a reality:

“Engineering work on the railway has already begun in Armenia, while construction of the highway and railway linking Azerbaijan with Armenia is nearly complete.”

He stressed that TRIPP is not simply an infrastructure project but also an important link in the Trans-Caspian trade route. It could drive new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries.

“It is a factor that opens up new trade opportunities for the United States and other countries. It is also an example of how economic cooperation can strengthen peace after long-standing disputes have been resolved,” Rubio said.

He added that peace had created an opportunity to deepen relations between the United States, Armenia and Azerbaijan. This, he said, would contribute to the economic prosperity of all three countries.

Thanks to Trump

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan thanked him for organising the peace summit and for signing the peace declaration adopted by the Armenian and Azerbaijani leaders as a testament to the agreement. He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: Live: Coalition demands AFP look at leaked melon gaffe correspondence
World.content:
The federal opposition has written to federal police urging them to investigate an apparent leak of correspondence over the prime minister's melon gaffe between Japan and Australia.

At least two Australian media outlets reported on Monday evening that a Japanese official had written to Australian counterparts last month, saying that Tokyo would not complain about the podcast exchange, and that media coverage of the incident was "sensationalised."

It's not clear who provided the correspondence to those outlets, but the Coalition is suggesting that the government may have orchestrated the leak in order to protect the prime minister.

Shadow Foreign Affairs Minister Ted O'Brien and Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson have now written to the AFP saying they're "concerned that a diplomatic note with a critical bilateral partner has potentially been provided to the media without authorisation."

World.title: Shut Sydney Chinatown cream puff eatery owes tax office $845,000
World.content:
The company behind Sydney Chinatown restaurant Emperor's Garden owes the tax office more than $845,000, court documents reveal.

The 47-year-old restaurant attracted long queues of customers lining up for cream puffs made fresh and sold cheap from a small takeaway window.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has applied to wind up Emperor's Garden Pty Ltd, arguing the company may be insolvent after chasing a tax debt of $845,133.11.

According to documents filed in the Federal Court, the ATO wants a liquidator appointed to the company and to have its costs paid from the company's assets.

A letter of demand was sent to the Haymarket restaurant in March.

Emperor's Garden Pty Ltd, run by Stanley and May Ho Yee, has not filed any documents with the Federal Court, and their son Valentine Yee, who is involved in running the Emperor's Garden restaurant, could not be contacted for comment.

Site earmarked for redevelopment

Plans had been made to redevelop the site. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The much-loved yum cha institution was mysteriously closed down earlier this month.

A sign on the Hay Street building said the property had been "lawfully re-entered and possession taken" with some inquiries directed to law firm Mills Oakley.

Mills Oakley had previously said it acted for one of the building's owners and declined to comment.

It is not clear who has taken possession of the site.

The building is co-owned by Mr and Mrs Yee and the company Hynsco, which lists Lance and Elaine Lai as directors. Mr Lai is Mr and Mrs Yee's nephew.

The Emperor's Garden site has conditional approval for a $44.5 million redevelopment that will transform the existing three-storey premises into a 16-storey complex containing 22 residential apartments.

The eatery was known for its cream puffs. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

A document prepared in support of the development application described Hynsco and Mr Lai's cousins Valentine Lee and Jonathan Lee as behind the plans.

Mr Lai could not be contacted for comment. Nor could Jonathan Yee.

A post on the Emperor's Garden Instagram page said the company's restaurant and bakery was "taking a small break" and "we'll be back soon".

The Emperor's Garden BBQ and Noodles restaurant on Thomas Street is still open.

The restaurant pictured at Haymarket in 1987. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

Operation Aero

Meanwhile, Valentine and Jonathan Yee are each facing charges in the NSW Supreme Court relating to an Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) investigation into a $100,000 donation to the Labor Party made by a prohibited donor.

The investigation, codenamed Operation Aero, found billionaire property developer Huang Xiangmo donated the cash, and Jonathan Yee, then involved with Chinese Friends of Labor, helped disguise the true origin of the money by organising for his mother, brother, several Emperor's Garden employees and To Yip of Harbour City Group to each sign a false donation declaration form.

Customers arrived at the restaurant to find it had closed. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Valentine Yee, his mother May Ho Yee and an Emperor's Garden employee, Wei Shi, have each been charged with giving false or misleading evidence to a public inquiry after appearing as witnesses at a 2019 hearing.

Valentine Yee has pleaded guilty to one count of giving false/misleading evidence at public inquiry, and Mr Shi has pleaded not guilty. Mrs Yee is yet to enter a plea.

Jonathan Yee has been charged with a raft of offences, including participation in a scheme to circumvent electoral funding laws, giving false evidence at a public inquiry and procuring false testimony at an inquiry.

He is yet to enter a plea.

World.title: Peaking inside the industrial kitchens cooking 80,000 meals for the troops
World.content:
Inside the Royal Australian Air Force Airmen's Mess in Darwin, dozens of chefs from all over the world are busy preparing thousands of meals.

The kitchen is one of four mess halls that have been temporarily scaled up by the Australian Defence Force (ADF) to support the country's largest aviation combat training activity, Exercise Pitch Black, in Northern Australia.

Over three weeks at the Darwin facilities alone, the ADF estimates a team of more than 80 military cooks from Canada, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Fiji and the United Kingdom served up a staggering 80,000 feeds — equating to 3,600 dishes a day.

Loading...

Typically, the 2,500 military personnel from 21 nations taking part are offered a dinnertime choice between goat, lamb, pork and beef, as well as two vegetarian options.

With crews participating in the exercise for weeks on end, New Zealand Army Private Liam Mischefski said the chefs tried to vary the options on the menu, which can range from curry to pasta.

The ABC has been given a rare behind-the-scenes glimpse into how chefs from air forces around the world, like Liam Mischefski, come together to cater for Exercise Pitch Black. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"It's very important obviously with religion, [and] dietary requirements come into play, so we have to make a lot of different meals to kind of provide for that," he said.

" With people spending so much time away from home, it's good for them to have a meal that kind of reminds them of where they came from and help them acclimatise to where they are. "

Private Mischefski said working with international chefs had allowed him to learn different cooking techniques and add recipes to his repertoire.

Plenty of extra chefs are hard at work in Darwin, ensuring all 2,500 meals are ready in time for each service. (ABC News)

"I've learnt different ways to make rice, I've learnt how the Australian mess operates — how they might cook their steaks, for example, and just the different degrees we cook our meats to," he said.

While preparing nutritional meals is the key to fuelling aviators, Private Mischefski said "fat boy Fridays" had been a popular night in the mess hall, with more hungry mouths showing up on the days fried food and steaks were on offer.

Variety of cuisines being prepared

While barramundi is one menu item flying the flag for local Top End produce, another notable Australian fixture that appears to be missing from the mix is Vegemite.

"I haven't seen any yet," Private Mischefski laughs.

Multiple Top End mess halls are serving thousands of military personnel from 21 nations, three times a day. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

The Aussie spread was not the only staple left out.

Despite not having his country's liquid gold on hand, Canadian Armed Forces Corporal Alex Bernier said he had enjoyed sharing familiar desserts from back home and trying new ones.

Alex Bernier enjoys sharing a little slice of Canada with the teams currently training in Darwin. (ABC News)

"We had a chance to do Nanaimo bars, sugar tarts, [but] unfortunately we don't have maple syrup either, so we do our best and people have enjoyed it so far — our own Canadian desserts," he said.

"My highlights would be of course working with the different countries, different nations' chefs.

"I think it's very rewarding, it's getting to [learn] their knowledge, experience and exchange from each other."

A lot of time, money and effort go into keeping all of the troops fed. (ABC News)

Royal New Zealand Navy leading chef Nadia Mwila echoed that sentiment, saying she would be taking home a recipe book full of new meals to cook when she returned.

"It's nice to meet different cultures from all around the world and take recipes, share your own way of doing things as well, especially all in one area," she said.

"They do some good curries here, so I've actually got a whole list that I've got emailed to me back home, [though I] haven't got to try them yet."

World.title: Health watchdog issues warning over second alleged fake Victorian doctor
World.content:
Victoria's health watchdog has banned a second alleged fake doctor from Melbourne's bayside from providing health services after he was accused of providing unapproved medications to treat a person's "significant" chronic illness.

The Health Complaints Commissioner has also issued a public warning about Maher (Michael) Aboudargham following an investigation launched last week.

The interim prohibition order bans him from providing any health service in Victoria for at least 12 weeks.

It comes after the watchdog took the same action against his alleged co-offender Ms Assma (Sarah) Samadi yesterday.

Last month, Victoria Police charged the pair with trafficking steroids after receiving reports claiming they were pretending to be medical practitioners in the Brighton East area, and allegedly charged more than $20,000 for their services since the start of the year in a series of "botched treatments," according to the force's statement.

Victoria Police said the alleged treatments include administering injections to a man with a long-term illness that were believed to assist with the illness, but other treatments allegedly contained common ingredients such as vitamins and protein powder.

Do you know more? Contact Antonia O'Flaherty at Oflaherty.Antonia@abc.net.au or on antoniaoflaherty@protonmail.com

The state's Health Complaints Commission (HCC) also received a report alleging the couple offered treatment they were not qualified to provide, unlawfully supplying unapproved medications to a person with a chronic illness, prompting them to investigate.

It's understood that report suggested the pair falsely represented Ms Samadi as a registered medical practitioner.

As the watchdog's investigation continues they are urging the public not to engage either of the pair to provide any health services and to come forward with any concerns they may have.

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner has issued an official warning against an alleged fake doctor in Melbourne's Bayside. (Health Complaints Commissioner)

The HCC Commissioner Bernice Redly said Victorians had a right to expect that anyone offering health services was appropriately qualified, honest about their credentials, and provided care that was safe and lawful.

"Where I believe there is a serious risk to the public, I will not hesitate to take action," the adjunct professor said.

"This public warning and interim prohibition order have been issued to protect the health and safety of the Victorian community while our investigation is ongoing."

Police arrested the 32-year-old woman and 39-year-old man at a unit in Brighton East on July 24, charging them with two counts of trafficking steroids, possessing cocaine, a drug of dependence and a schedule 4 poison, common law assault and obtaining property by deception.

Detectives searched the Brighton East unit and also a Caulfield North apartment, uncovering what police alleged was a stash of cocaine and significant quantities of prescription medications such as testosterone, synthetic anabolic steroids, pain killers and human growth hormones.

The pair were released on bail and are set to appear in court in October.

World.title: Police launch murder probe into woman's death in Logan
World.content:
Police have launched a murder probe into the death of a woman in her 20s in Logan overnight.

Emergency services were called to a property at Slacks Creek around 12:30am, where the woman was found unresponsive and declared dead.

A 37-year-old Slacks Creek man was arrested at the property and is helping police.

The man and woman knew each other.

Police said there is no threat to the community.

World.title: Fraser confirms intentions for Carlton coaching job after hot streak
World.content:
Carlton caretaker Josh Fraser wants the full-time coaching job.

Fraser has told Carlton hierarchy he is keen to become the permanent head coach after his stunning success as interim boss.

The former Collingwood ruckman has won 10 of 12 games since the departure of Michael Voss and is now among five candidates for the permanent job.

Fraser, 44, initially said he wasn't interested in being the full-time coach from next season.

Carlton has won 10 out of 12 games under Fraser's guidance, surging into finals contention. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

But he has changed his mind after his blistering start to coaching, and now appears the frontrunner in a field of five.

Fremantle's Jaymie Graham, St Kilda's Corey Enright, Geelong's James Kelly — all current assistant coaches — have interviewed for the role, along with Hawthorn's head of development Daniel Giansiracusa.

Fraser's about-turn comes as he revives the on-field fortunes of the Blues, who were languishing with one win and eight losses when Voss departed in mid-May.

Carlton appears set for a wildcard finals berth, sitting 10th on the ladder and two wins clear of 11th-placed St Kilda with two rounds remaining.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Blues meet the Western Bulldogs on Sunday before their last home-and-away game against ladder-leaders Fremantle.

Fraser, who played 200 games with Collingwood and 18 at Gold Coast, began his coaching career as coach of the Suns' state league side.

He then coached Carlton and Collingwood at VFL level before returning to the Blues as an assistant to Voss this season.

Two weeks ago, Carlton's football boss Chris Davies said the club wanted Fraser to apply for the full-time role.

"We think he should put his hand up," Davies said at the time.

Since those comments, Fraser has overseen a 76-point thrashing of reigning premiers Brisbane and a 44-point victory over the Saints.

AAP

World.title: Trump's secret plane switch sparks debate over missile 'decoy' passengers
World.content:
Ethical questions have been raised about a US Secret Service ruse that used a plane full of journalists as a possible "decoy" in response to an alleged Iranian threat to shoot Air Force One out of the sky.

The Washington Post yesterday revealed US President Donald Trump secretly climbed off the plane and into an airport catering truck minutes after he was filmed boarding the aircraft in Türkiye in July.

The president was moved after the US received intelligence from Israel about an Iranian threat to use shoulder-to-air missiles to target the plane, the Wall Street Journal reported today.

The plane then left Türkiye, which borders Iran, carrying members of the media and some White House staff who had been in Ankara with the president for a NATO summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also stayed on the plane, according to an unnamed US official who spoke to the Journal.

"Everyone on that plane was a decoy," prominent political analyst and Democratic strategist David Axelrod told CNN.

"If they felt that it was unsafe to be on the plane, then it was unsafe for everybody else to be on the plane as well."

The White House has not challenged the reports. It responded to the Post's report with a statement that said in part: "As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats."

Mr Trump has not yet commented. Mr Rubio ignored a reporter's question about the operation as he posed for photographs at the State Department today.

Ned Price, a State Department advisor during the Biden administration, said he had travelled overseas with multiple presidents and recognised that "subterfuge is sometimes a necessary safeguard".

"But misleading reporters in the moment and, worse yet, continuing to lie to the American people weeks later is never acceptable," he wrote on X.

"As far as I know, it's unique to this White House."

Iran war has spread beyond one strait The Middle East conflict isn't just widening, it's highlighting more vulnerabilities in the region.

The use of "backup planes" to protect the US president from threats is not unusual, said University of New Haven protective travel expert Robert McDonald, who was a Secret Service agent for more than 20 years.

"Everywhere the president travels overseas, there's always a backup plane," he told Reuters.

But he said the "decoy" plane would also have been well protected.

"Were the press decoys on the other plane? I'm willing to bet there were plenty of assets in and around those two 747s flying from Turkey to England, whether it be Air Force, allied air forces, different capabilities," he said.

"Nobody let the press dangle out there or the other members of the White House staff. They were all part of that plan."

Mr Trump had flown to Ankara, Türkiye, on a new Air Force One plane that had been gifted to the US by Qatar. It was the jet's first international presidential trip.

But at the NATO summit, Mr Trump announced he would depart Ankara on an older Air Force One plane "for old time's sake". It was later reported the newer Air Force One plane lacked some of the defensive security features of the older jet.

Mr Trump boarded the older plane in Ankara in view of TV cameras. But the Post reported he was secretly shuttled to a smaller Air Force C-32A via a truck that is typically used to load meals and other supplies before a flight.

The reporters who were still aboard the older Air Force One plane were not made aware of the extent of the threat to the flight, the Post reported, citing a US official.

World.title: 'Dare to Dream' project combats lack of queer spaces in Sydney's west
World.content:
Amid the hustle of shoppers in Parramatta, an art installation with personal shrines symbolises an oasis for the queer and gender diverse community seeking visibility and acceptance.

The Rainbow Crossing has been a signifier of LGBTQIA+ acceptance in Sydney for years, but members of Greater Western Sydney's community say these safe spaces are difficult to come by west of the CBD.

Artist Bonnie Huang's work, Dare to Dream, is a multimedia art program which combats this by tying the experiences of LGBTQ+ people in the area with cultural heritage.

"There are a lot of cultural nuances, even religious nuances, within our community and everyone's different backgrounds, so there's definitely an element of balancing different backgrounds and different cultural needs," they said.

Huang with their art installation at Westfield Parramatta. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Connection through collaboration

Huang worked with the C3West program at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia and ACON Westie, a social community for queer and gender diverse people in Western Sydney, to host gatherings.

Mr de Almeida says about 70 people previously not known to each other worked on the project. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

MCA senior curator Pedro de Almeida said the program aimed to bring artists and communities together to "address local concerns".

"Over a period of nine months, we engaged with people from Mount Druitt, Bankstown, Blacktown, Parramatta, Granville," Mr de Almeida said.

"Dare to Dream essentially attracted a cohort of about 70 community members all unknown to each other."

Huang led participants at gatherings to create sculptures of personal shrines which were embedded into the installation at Westfield Parramatta.

"A key part of my experience as a queer person living in Western Sydney was this sense of loneliness and wanting to find other people like me, but also wanting to find spaces where we could be together," Huang said.

"We connected over this desire of wanting to find each other in the places where we grew up, or even the fact that a lot of us moved out of Western Sydney in order for us to find explicitly queer spaces."

A balancing act

Drag queen Kaia Papaya says she found more of a community in the CBD, rather than in Western Sydney. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

Drag queen Kaia Papaya grew up in Sydney's south-west and used to travel upwards of two hours a day to study at the University of New South Wales.

"There were obviously a lot more gay spaces in universities as well, but we just didn't have time to attend those," she said.

Papaya said she found more of a community in her early 20s in Sydney's CBD.

"At least 10 years ago, there weren't any spaces in the west … we were literally meeting each other at night time, like 8pm onwards, and it was pretty dangerous," she said.

Papaya says it will take time for Western Sydney to become more accepting of queer people. (ABC News: Marcus Stimson)

Papaya hoped in the future, queerness would become "readily accepted" in cultural settings.

"It's a great way to break the ice, not only for the younger generation, but obviously for the parents … where it's not so much a taboo topic," she said.

"Even something as small as the Lunar New Year festivals, something that holds true to the cultures that live around those areas."

She said "it would take time" for Western Sydney to catch up with the open acceptance of queerness, like in the CBD.

Where queerness and culture overlap

ACON's Duy Tran says safe spaces need to be incorporated within cultural spaces. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Duy Tran from ACON Westie said the sheer geographical size of Western Sydney posed a challenge to improved access to queer spaces.

"There isn't a centralised queer space here like there is in the inner city, and a lot of communities are quite isolated, and they feel like they don't have a place to be able to be themselves," Mr Tran said.

" Because there hasn't been a lot of those spaces that really speak to the multicultural and LGBTQ+ side of things in tandem, there hasn't been an opportunity for community to develop. "

Mr Tran said, due to safety concerns, some queer people in Western Sydney turned to more "discreet" approaches to access services or safe spaces, but said this was slowly changing.

"If you compare it to even two years ago, things are looking a lot more different now," he said.

"I think [safe spaces] need to be incorporated within cultural spaces.

"I feel like when you bring culture along, and bring people along, and bring our family along, and bring your parents along, they are a lot more receptive than you think."

World.title: ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency Michael Koziol August 12, 2026 — 6:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump delivered a cryptic response when asked whether he would consider calling a national security emergency ahead of the midterm elections, giving oxygen to calls from right-wing pundits for an unprecedented intervention. The US president was asked on Real America’s Voice – a conservative media network that includes former Trump strategist Steve Bannon – about the prospects of him declaring such an emergency within the next month. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office this week. Bloomberg “Let me just say this, stranger things have happened. I’ll leave it at that,” Trump replied. The host, Wayne Allyn Root, one of the prominent advocates for the idea, agreed to leave the subject there. The comments mark the first time Trump has engaged with the specific proposal for a national security emergency ahead of the November midterms – an idea pushed by Bannon, Root and other influential pundits in recent months.



It comes amid the US Senate’s refusal to pass the SAVE Act, a bill that would compel prospective voters to show documentary proof of American citizenship in person when registering to vote and present photo ID at the polling booth. Currently, voter ID requirements differ from state to state. Root said the emergency declaration would deliver photo ID and proof of citizenship requirements, plus restrictions on mail-in ballots, which Trump has also advocated. Later, when he described it as “the SAVE Act on steroids”, Trump said: “Yep.” Journalist John Solomon, right, has been made a special government employee in the White House examining election integrity and alleged weaponisation. Bloomberg Chuck Schumer, the Democrats’ Senate leader, noted the remarks. “Donald Trump wants to take over American elections,” he said. “Senate Democrats are prepared to combat his unprecedented, illegal efforts at every turn.” Last month, in a much-hyped prime-time address to the nation, Trump unveiled what he said was evidence of widespread election meddling and influence by China, including the alleged harvesting of 220 million Americans’ data.



“Members of the deep state” within the US intelligence system actively worked to suppress and downplay the seriousness of this activity, Trump claimed on national television. The allegations attracted scepticism throughout the American media and were generally seen as lacking evidence or rehashing known vulnerabilities in the electoral system. Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser, has been one of the key voices calling for a national security emergency. Bloomberg But they were immediately used by Trump’s conservative media backers as justification for the president to intervene in the democratic process. Bannon told this masthead that same evening: “The damning evidence unearthed from the ‘deep state’ intelligence agencies sets the predicate for President Trump to declare a national security emergency regarding this November’s elections.”



Later, he said Trump’s televised address was the beginning of the process, and more evidence of election fraud would be presented. “I believe we will have a national emergency declared by late August.” Over the past week, the White House has attempted to focus attention on declassified documents showing the FBI opened a criminal probe into Trump in May 2017 to examine whether he acted – wittingly or unwittingly – as a Russian asset when he fired then FBI director James Comey. Trade counsellor Peter Navarro, a loyal Trump ally, spoke at length about the allegations at the White House on Tuesday morning. Bloomberg It is part of a broader investigation by the White House into election integrity and the alleged weaponisation of the federal government against Trump by the so-called “deep state”. That probe is being run by John Solomon, founder of right-wing news site Just The News, who has been brought into the White House temporarily as a special government employee.



Related Article Opinion

Steve Bannon Trump will declare a ‘national emergency’ before midterms: Bannon Peter Hartcher Political and international editor On Tuesday morning (US time), the president’s loyal trade counsellor, Peter Navarro, spoke to reporters at the White House at length about the allegations, and called for Republicans in US Congress to immediately issue subpoenas. “These people need to be held to account,” he said. “This was nothing more than an attempted coup d’tat.” Navarro – who went to jail in 2024 for refusing to co-operate with a congressional probe into the January 6, 2021 riots at the US Capitol – declined to talk about his discussions with Trump on the matter, citing executive privilege. “If you look at the president’s statements, he wants, as Steve Bannon said, action, action, action,” Navarro said. “There’s nothing more important than election integrity.”

World.title: Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback
World.content:
CultureMusicPerforming arts Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback Nick Galvin August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After several years plagued by management volatility and financial strife, Opera Australia is pitching its 2027 season as one of stability and renewed ambition with a varied slate of productions for Sydney and Melbourne. The new season ranges from a new David McVicar production of Wagner’s Tannhäuser to a family-friendly, steampunk Magic Flute, two major Australian operas and the return of Gilbert and Sullivan to the Sydney Opera House. Amy Lane and Ruth Thomas. James Brickwood This will be the first season for newly appointed director of opera Amy Lane, who is presently serving out her time as artistic director of the Copenhagen Opera Festival. She will join OA full time after delivering her final event in Denmark this month and said she was excited for the company’s future. “It does feel strangely like, after a slightly bumpy period, that the ground is kind of fertile for us to go, ‘OK, what are we planting and what are we going to see in our five-year round?’” she said. Lane joins Alex Budd (CEO) and music director Andrea Battistoni in a revamped leadership team, wiping the slate clean from the revolving-door era of Jo Davies and Fiona Allan.



The big-ticket item for 2027 will be staged not in the Sydney Opera House but at Melbourne’s State Theatre, which will come as a relief to the city’s opera fans, who have suffered slim pickings for the past three years while the venue has been closed for renovations. Performers in the steampunk take on The Magic Flute by Scottish Opera. Tannhäuser is a monumental work requiring an orchestra too big for the pit at the Opera House’s Joan Sutherland theatre – not to mention the massive off-stage brass ensemble scored by Wagner. OA will be hoping fans from Sydney and beyond will make the trip to Melbourne to see Scottish director McVicar’s vision for Tannhäuser. “His take on it is so extraordinary,” said Lane. “Only David’s mind could work in this brilliant way to find a pathway through this piece to make it enticing, not just for those who love Wagner, but for those who want to be in the theatre.” Leah Purcell with composer of The Drover’s Wife, George Palmer. Sam Mooy



She described initial meetings with McVicar, where he outlined his vision for Tannhäuser as “exhilarating”. In Sydney, OA is pitching the Australian premiere of Scottish Opera’s well-reviewed Magic Flute as a show for all ages in its continuing bid to capture young opera fans. Opera Australia hopes a steampunk take on Magic Flute will excite younger audiences. James Glossop “We’re trying to program family operas and build on that,” said planning and program director Ruth Thomas. “We had Hansel and Gretel earlier this year and last year we had Cendrillon [Cinderella] so we want to try and keep that [going].” Sydney’s season opens with the local premiere of perhaps the world’s best-loved opera, Puccini’s La Boheme, which has its world premiere in Melbourne in November. Sydney audiences also get a return of Simon Phillips’ production of Donizetti’s frothy comic opera The Elixir of Love, complete with ocker-ised surtitles.



Also coming to Sydney is an intriguing double-bill of one-act French works. Ravel’s L’enfant et les sortileges will feature much-loved Australian mezzo soprano Margaret Plummer. La Voix humaine, by Francis Poulenc, is a one-woman opera in which the woman makes a final phone call with her faithless lover. Leah Purcell at Opera Australia’s headquarters. Sam Mooy “You hear her side of the conversation as we as an audience have to imagine what she is hearing,” said Lane. “It is painfully intimate and so vulnerable.” Sydney’s winter season features a return of McVicar’s lush production of Faust plus Stuart Maunder’s knockabout Pirates of Penzance and a Sydney premiere of Verdi’s A Masked Ball. Melbourne also gets that city’s premiere of Ann Yee’s Turandot, the Magic Flute and Leah Purcell’s stunning The Drover’s Wife. And in a left-field programming decision, Melbourne fans will get a one-off performance of Beethoven’s 9th Symphony with the Opera Australia Chorus and Orchestra Victoria.

World.title: Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCompetition Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare David Swan August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Small businesses’ online shops are being switched off by computer algorithms with no warning or apparent human oversight, the small business ombudsman’s office says, as digital platform disputes become its biggest source of complaints. These disputes have quadrupled to 48.3 per cent of all new cases managed by the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman in the June quarter, up from 12 per cent a year earlier. Businesses built over a decade or more, with millions of dollars a year in sales running through their online accounts, can now be closed off in seconds by a system nobody has to explain, the agency warns. Jack Nekhala, inventor of the Bed Scrunchie. Sellers increasingly report their accounts being switched off entirely, rather than the isolated problems that once dominated: a hacked login, a withheld payment, a single listing pulled down. “Small businesses seeking our assistance describe how a ‘community standards’ algorithm has taken down their account without any apparent human oversight,” the ombudsman’s office told this masthead.



Last month, at least five Melbourne and Sydney queer venues were locked out of Facebook and Instagram accounts they had spent more than a decade building, with the stated reasons ranging from human exploitation to a review over alleged drugs and guns. Meta later said the accounts had been flagged in error. A suspension freezes a company’s account on such platforms, cutting sellers off from customer details and product photographs. The ombudsman’s office has urged digital platforms to provide human contacts, specific reasons and structured appeal paths before taking such action. Nekhala has lodged a complaint against Amazon with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). AP One of the disputes has recently been taken to the competition watchdog: US inventor Jack Nekhala has lodged a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) against Amazon Commercial Services, the online giant’s local arm, after his amazon.com.au seller account was deactivated on April 11, 2025. He says there had been no Australian investigation or notice, and is asking the ACCC to establish whether anyone in Australia had assessed the decision or if it automatically followed a US block.



Nekhala invented the ‘Bed Scrunchie’, a sheet fastener business that turned over about $US6 million ($8.5 million) a year, almost all through Amazon. Trouble began in September 2024, when Amazon accepted two patent infringement complaints against the product. Nekhala’s listing was disabled for nine days and took 19 calls to Amazon support. The fix, which he eventually found in a two-year-old Reddit post rather than from Amazon, was to formally retract a complaint he says he never lodged. Then, on October 30 that year, Amazon deactivated Nekhala’s US, Canadian, Mexican and Brazilian accounts over alleged review rule breaches - the platform’s guidelines for consumer feedback, testimonials and online ratings, with nine European marketplaces following days later. Related Article Social media Queer venues locked out as Meta suspensions hit Melbourne and Sydney Weeks later, a man on LinkedIn offering Temu sales support connected Nekhala to a woman calling herself Jenna, who said she was a bedding seller with contacts inside Amazon. She was not an Amazon employee, and Nekhala says he never dealt with one directly. Over four calls, Jenna showed him internal Amazon material about his account, including enforcement classifications and investigator notes invisible to standard sellers. The records described his account block as final with an instruction not to disclose the investigation’s reason to the seller. This masthead has reviewed Nekhala’s complaint records, correspondence with Amazon and his submission to the ACCC.



Jenna offered to have an internal contact release roughly $US90,000 in frozen funds for a 20 per cent fee. Nekhala says he refused to pay, but kept the conversation going to understand the offer. “If confidential account information can leave Amazon, or if intermediaries can sell supposed influence over suspensions, complaints, reviews, listings, or frozen funds, honest Australian sellers may be competing in a marketplace where the official rules are not the only rules,” he said. Amazon said the account was permanently suspended following multiple enforcement actions for policy violations. Asked about the case by Bloomberg in June, Amazon confirmed the employee who leaked Nekhala’s information had been sacked for unrelated misconduct. A spokesman said employee involvement in fraud is very rare, and Amazon invests heavily in prevention. Nekhala says Amazon has never named the employee, provided access logs, or said whether other sellers were affected. Contacted by this masthead, Amazon confirmed that Nekhala’s account had been suspended for policy violations, without providing further details. It rejected the entrepreneur’s account that it was because it found his warranty cards, which offered customers a free accessory in exchange for registering and leaving a review, amounted to review manipulation. Nekhala says the reviews were published on his own website, weren’t linked to Amazon and never required a positive rating.



Independent sellers account for more than 60 per cent of Amazon’s global sales and thousands of Australian businesses, most of them small and medium-sized, sell in its stores, according to the online retail behemoth. Professor Jeannie Paterson of Melbourne University Law School University of Melbourne Australian sellers have several routes to support, Amazon says, including phone, email and live chats, with access to Selling Partner Support and account health specialists. Email support runs around the clock, while phone and live chat are handled between 9am and 6pm. Whether local consumer law can protect Nekhala’s contract is contested. A seller’s account being immediately deactivated due to a platform’s own risk assessment, with financial consequences and no disclosed reason, could be unfair under the Australian Consumer Law, according to University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson. “A service provider can terminate at will, but generally needs sound reasons for doing this and ideally criteria for when it will take place,” she said.



Nekhala’s Australian revenue was modest, at $US31,444 in 2023. After the shutdown, about 650 stranded bed scrunchies were handed to a distributor. The product now reaches Australian shoppers through that distributor at $99.99, up from Nekhala’s direct $79.99 price. University of Sydney academic Rob Nicholls said complaints of this kind hinge on whether they reveal a systemic problem. “If this problem has also affected a number of other, likely Australian, small businesses, then the ACCC will be concerned,” he said. The ACCC said it does not comment on complaints it receives, or on individual businesses. A spokesman said obligations under the Australian Consumer Law applied equally to every business trading in Australia, whether based here or overseas, and that whether particular conduct breached the law depended on the circumstances. “The ACCC has consistently been advocating for adequate mandatory minimum standards for digital platforms’ internal dispute resolution, and an independent external dispute resolution body for digital platform services,” a spokesman said. World.title: Four minutes of silence and an unexpected gift: Inside the ACO’s eclectic new program
World.content:
CultureMusicPerforming arts Four minutes of silence and an unexpected gift: Inside the ACO’s eclectic new program Nick Galvin August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Adams, one of the world’s most influential living composers, was part way through arranging a string quartet for the Australian Chamber Orchestra when he had a sudden change of heart. “No, damn it,” the ACO’s Richard Tognetti recalls Adams deciding. “I’m going to write them a piece – a whole piece.” Richard Tognetti is still proud to be labelled an enfant terrible. Sitthixay Ditthavong The result is Gioia, a new work from the master composer created specifically for Tognetti and principal violin Satu Vanska. “Suddenly we have this extraordinary piece written for us,” says Tognetti. “We’re touring it next year in Australia and the United States. It’s the only piece he’s writing in his 80th year.”



Adams’ generous gift will be one of the highlights of a 2027 season that ranges across J. S. Bach, Part, Cage, Reich and Richard Strauss, as well as Mozart, Haydn and Schubert. Another marquee event of the ACO’s 52nd season will be an intimate performance of Bach’s transcendent St John Passion in a collaboration with award-winning Belgian vocal ensemble Vox Luminis. “The St John Passion, it’s got the whole world in it and more,” says Tognetti. “How astonishing that this dude J. S. Bach, all on his own up there in northern Germany, ends up creating music that makes him the greatest composer who ever lived.” And if the 18th-century German master were somehow to be present in the City Recital Hall to hear the ACO’s performance, what might he think? ACO principal violin Satu Vanska is one of the dedicatees of Adams’ new work. Charlie Kinross



“He’d certainly recognise it and I think he’d be delighted,” says Tognetti. “And I think he’d be surprised that his work has astral-travelled through the ages and [is] being played in this strange land of which he wasn’t even aware. Like any composer, he should be delighted his music is being kept alive.” In June the ACO will also stage its first festival, a four-day event in its Walsh Bay HQ. Entitled Currents, the event will bring together a series of eclectic programs ranging from Missy Mazzoli and Samuel Adams (son of John) to Mozart and Bach. As part of Currents, audiences will also get the chance to witness John Cage’s 4′33″, the American composer’s infamous (or revelatory, depending on your point of view) work consisting only of silence. “I did it in Maribor [Slovenia] and I tried to do it in the Adelaide Festival recently,” says Tognetti. “It’s always … a failed attempt at the exploration of nothingness. “It’s seriously confronting, on a par with trying to get a kid to meditate. You start noticing sounds in your head in the hall. Some people giggle, nervous giggles. Some people just hate it. The Brookner-loving 72-year-old classical music fan wants to kill you. And some people really find something revelatory about it.”



The 2027 season will close with the mouthwatering prospect of young soprano Masabane Cecilia Rangwanasha’s Australian debut performing Richard Strauss’ sublime Four Last Songs with an expanded ACO. Editor's pick Performing arts ‘It’s a beautiful instrument’: The young virtuoso who learnt by hugging a cello The season is classic Tognetti, by turns intriguing, challenging and revelatory. However, with him recently turning 61, I wonder whether the ACO director can still claim the badge of “enfant terrible” routinely applied to him down the years? “I think you’re born a certain age,” he says. “I’ve always sort of felt 17, so the answer is, ‘Yes, you can’. “I think the proof of the pudding is that I still get really exasperated by people if they’re not trying to get everything they possibly can from every second of every day. I’m a bit of a hard taskmaster like that.



“And with so-called classical music – and don’t we hate that expression – if a performance comes across as being in aspic, I also get exasperated.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty; CBA results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty; CBA results ahead Stan Choe August 12, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped a bit further from their records, while oil prices kept swinging on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for a second modest drop since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 184 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.6 per cent. Rising oil prices weighed on Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6am pointing to a loss of 37 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Tuesday. Commonwealth Banks results are the highlight of reporting season today. The Australian dollar is trading at US70.60¢. The action was stronger in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly jumped above $US90 in the morning before falling back below $US87. It eventually settled at $US88.91, up 1.4 per cent from Monday.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such erratic moves have become typical since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and kept much of the world’s oil pent up in the Middle East. Last month alone, Brent’s price veered between $US72 and $US102 per barrel. Higher oil prices make inflation worse, and they’ve sent the average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to $US4.01, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US3.14 a year ago, though it’s down from last week’s nearly $US4.09. That has Wall Street’s attention focused on Wednesday, when the US government will release the latest monthly reading on inflation. Economists expect it to show inflation remains high but that it decelerated to 3.4 per cent in July from 3.5 per cent in June. That could help the Federal Reserve, whose members are notably split on whether they should be raising the country’s interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. While higher rates could help slow the increases of prices on store shelves, they would also slow the overall US economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



Traders are betting on a coin flip’s chance that the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group. If it does, that would be the first increase in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates. Treasury yields have jumped since the war with Iran because of higher oil prices and worries about inflation, sending long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. The 10-year Treasury yield eased back Tuesday, falling to 4.69 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday. But it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. On Wall Street, On Holding dropped 20.3 per cent even though the Swiss sneaker company reported a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for upcoming revenue that fell short of analysts’ expectations, while saying it does not want to slash prices to drum up more sales. Companies broadly have been blowing past analysts’ forecasts, which Wall Street loves because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. Earnings per share for S&P 500 companies are on track to be 50 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet, and that’s a big reason US stocks have been setting records recently despite worries about expensive oil, high inflation and other challenges.



Aramark, the food company and facilities manager, rallied 8.5 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Cardinal Health added 1.3 per cent after topping analysts’ profit expectations for the spring. Related Article Opinion

The Dow Jones Industrial dropped 184.13 to 53,791.85, and the Nasdaq composite sank 159.91 to 26,445.45. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia.
