World.title: There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one? Kaye Fallick August 12, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When compulsory super was introduced by the Keating Labor government in 1992, few predicted the extraordinary growth of total superannuation savings to the nearly $5 trillion it represents today. Initially, most workers joined the fund suggested by their employer. Fast-forward to 2026, and there is more complexity and a wider range of differently structured super funds from which to select. Few could have predicted the runaway success of superannuation. Simon Letch It’s important to keep abreast of your options by fully understanding the type of fund you’re in, and whether it’s time to review other options, and if so, what you need to consider. The following covers the three broad types of fund, with a note on two others. Read on to identify your fund type and what it delivers.



1. Choice funds Editor's pick Opinion

Retirement living The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong Bec Wilson Money contributor As the name suggests, a choice fund is a super fund that the member chooses. Let’s say you start your first job at the local ice-cream store. It’s compulsory for the employer to pay 12 per cent of your wage into the super fund of your choice. They may recommend one that suits your industry. But you can instruct your employer to contribute your super to any other fund you prefer. If you don’t do this, your employer can assign your savings into a MySuper option – a default fund for those who have not selected a fund or investment settings. A government initiative, MySuper has been designed as a simple, low-fee solution for those who don’t want to make active decisions about their super. Choice funds can be divided into two general categories: industry funds or retail funds.



Industry funds: As the name suggests, industry funds originally represented a band of workers doing a specific type of work, such as hospitality, transport or teaching in universities. Initially closed to other workers, most are now public offer funds, meaning anyone can join. The names of the funds have evolved to reflect this change, from industry-specific to brands such as Aware, Brighter and Australian Retirement Trust. Industry funds operate as “profit-to-member” funds and have fees set low to deliver more benefits to members. It’s possible that you could establish any one of these types of funds. It’s unlikely all would suit your personal financial situation. Retail funds: Retail funds, by comparison, were traditionally offered by banks or insurance companies. These funds were always open to any members – i.e. public offering. Some are profit-to- member, but some are “for-profit” (earnings are distributed to the company and shareholders). For many years, as industry funds gained weight in members and funds under management, retail funds showed less impressive returns. More recently, the retail funds have lowered their fees, and new entries such as Vanguard are targeting younger members.



As with the industry funds, many are also developing hybrid digital advice support. Both industry and retail super funds are regulated by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA). 2. Platform funds Also known as wrap, or master trusts, these funds offer a distinctly different member experience. While you can open a direct individual account with some, most platforms encourage members to join through a financial adviser. Platforms vary from industry and super funds because they offer a platform or administrative system that allows the saver/investor member to combine management of shares, super and other investments, including property, and receive one consolidated report. Fees for platform funds are generally higher than those for industry and retail funds, and ongoing advice consultations are usually encouraged. They are regulated by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).



Recent research by Connexus Institute shows a major outflow over the past 12 months from choice funds to platform funds, particularly Netwealth and Hub24. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m in my 40s with $300,000 in super. Should I start an SMSF? Noel Whittaker Money columnist 3. Self-managed super funds (SMSFs) Successfully running an SMSF is not for the faint-hearted. Yes, many will suggest that they are easy to set up – but the point of super is not to start, but to finish well – i.e. to maximise your wealth at a better rate than if it was in another type of fund. Unlike choice funds, SMSFs are overseen by two regulators: the Australian Taxation Office (for compliance with super and tax laws) and ASIC for financial advice and auditors.



There are 661,000 SMSFs in Australia, covering 1.22 million members (7.2 per cent of all super fund members but 25 per cent of the pool of super savings) often held by high net worth people and business owners. One question frequently asked is: at which point does it become viable to establish an SMSF? The amount varies according to whoever is replying – but it’s generally agreed that below a $250,000 balance, the costs will outweigh the benefits. The average starting balance, according to accountancy group, H&R Block, is $400,000. Establishing a SMSF is not for the faint-hearted. Louie Douvis Apart from the fees associated with establishment of an SMSF and annual running costs, the most important requirement is that, as a trustee, you have the time, expertise and diligence to actively manage your fund. Or if you don’t, you have access to a qualified professional who can do this for you. There are two other fund types that are less common. These are public sector funds, which are available to government employees, and corporate sector funds, which are generally set up by a company for its employees only.



Which fund is right for you? While it’s possible that you could join or establish any one of these types of funds, it’s unlikely all would suit your personal financial situation. It’s important that your fund is closely aligned with your: level of savings

complexity of income, assets and investments

expectation of returns

needs and goals

preferred level or involvement, and therefore

your required level of support. Where to find out more? The Moneysmart website offers a useful summary of the features and benefits of different types of super fund. For more detail on platforms, the overview on SuperGuide is helpful. Kaye Fallick is an author, publisher, commentator and retirement income “explainer”, as well as co-creator of the Retirement Affordability Index.

World.title: ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS election ‘Stranger things have happened’: Trump coy on calling midterm-elections emergency Michael Koziol August 12, 2026 — 6:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump delivered a cryptic response when asked whether he would consider calling a national security emergency ahead of the midterm elections, giving oxygen to calls from right-wing pundits for an unprecedented intervention. The US president was asked on Real America’s Voice – a conservative media network that includes former Trump strategist Steve Bannon – about the prospects of him declaring such an emergency within the next month. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office this week. Bloomberg “Let me just say this, stranger things have happened. I’ll leave it at that,” Trump replied. The host, Wayne Allyn Root, one of the prominent advocates for the idea, agreed to leave the subject there. The comments mark the first time Trump has engaged with the specific proposal for a national security emergency ahead of the November midterms – an idea pushed by Bannon, Root and other influential pundits in recent months.



It comes amid the US Senate’s refusal to pass the SAVE Act, a bill that would compel prospective voters to show documentary proof of American citizenship in person when registering to vote and present photo ID at the polling booth. Currently, voter ID requirements differ from state to state. Root said the emergency declaration would deliver photo ID and proof of citizenship requirements, plus restrictions on mail-in ballots, which Trump has also advocated. Later, when he described it as “the SAVE Act on steroids”, Trump said: “Yep.” Journalist John Solomon, right, has been made a special government employee in the White House examining election integrity and alleged weaponisation. Bloomberg Chuck Schumer, the Democrats’ Senate leader, noted the remarks. “Donald Trump wants to take over American elections,” he said. “Senate Democrats are prepared to combat his unprecedented, illegal efforts at every turn.” Last month, in a much-hyped prime-time address to the nation, Trump unveiled what he said was evidence of widespread election meddling and influence by China, including the alleged harvesting of 220 million Americans’ data.



“Members of the deep state” within the US intelligence system actively worked to suppress and downplay the seriousness of this activity, Trump claimed on national television. The allegations attracted scepticism throughout the American media and were generally seen as lacking evidence or rehashing known vulnerabilities in the electoral system. Steve Bannon, a former Trump adviser, has been one of the key voices calling for a national security emergency. Bloomberg But they were immediately used by Trump’s conservative media backers as justification for the president to intervene in the democratic process. Bannon told this masthead that same evening: “The damning evidence unearthed from the ‘deep state’ intelligence agencies sets the predicate for President Trump to declare a national security emergency regarding this November’s elections.”



Later, he said Trump’s televised address was the beginning of the process, and more evidence of election fraud would be presented. “I believe we will have a national emergency declared by late August.” Over the past week, the White House has attempted to focus attention on declassified documents showing the FBI opened a criminal probe into Trump in May 2017 to examine whether he acted – wittingly or unwittingly – as a Russian asset when he fired then FBI director James Comey. Trade counsellor Peter Navarro, a loyal Trump ally, spoke at length about the allegations at the White House on Tuesday morning. Bloomberg It is part of a broader investigation by the White House into election integrity and the alleged weaponisation of the federal government against Trump by the so-called “deep state”. That probe is being run by John Solomon, founder of right-wing news site Just The News, who has been brought into the White House temporarily as a special government employee.



Related Article Opinion

Steve Bannon Trump will declare a ‘national emergency’ before midterms: Bannon Peter Hartcher Political and international editor On Tuesday morning (US time), the president’s loyal trade counsellor, Peter Navarro, spoke to reporters at the White House at length about the allegations, and called for Republicans in US Congress to immediately issue subpoenas. “These people need to be held to account,” he said. “This was nothing more than an attempted coup d’tat.” Navarro – who went to jail in 2024 for refusing to co-operate with a congressional probe into the January 6, 2021 riots at the US Capitol – declined to talk about his discussions with Trump on the matter, citing executive privilege. “If you look at the president’s statements, he wants, as Steve Bannon said, action, action, action,” Navarro said. “There’s nothing more important than election integrity.”

World.title: Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback
World.content:
CultureMusicPerforming arts Too big for Sydney: This massive work signals Opera Australia’s comeback Nick Galvin August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After several years plagued by management volatility and financial strife, Opera Australia is pitching its 2027 season as one of stability and renewed ambition with a varied slate of productions for Sydney and Melbourne. The new season ranges from a new David McVicar production of Wagner’s Tannhäuser to a family-friendly, steampunk Magic Flute, two major Australian operas and the return of Gilbert and Sullivan to the Sydney Opera House. Amy Lane and Ruth Thomas. James Brickwood This will be the first season for newly appointed director of opera Amy Lane, who is presently serving out her time as artistic director of the Copenhagen Opera Festival. She will join OA full time after delivering her final event in Denmark this month and said she was excited for the company’s future. “It does feel strangely like, after a slightly bumpy period, that the ground is kind of fertile for us to go, ‘OK, what are we planting and what are we going to see in our five-year round?’” she said. Lane joins Alex Budd (CEO) and music director Andrea Battistoni in a revamped leadership team, wiping the slate clean from the revolving-door era of Jo Davies and Fiona Allan.



The big-ticket item for 2027 will be staged not in the Sydney Opera House but at Melbourne’s State Theatre, which will come as a relief to the city’s opera fans, who have suffered slim pickings for the past three years while the venue has been closed for renovations. Performers in the steampunk take on The Magic Flute by Scottish Opera. Tannhäuser is a monumental work requiring an orchestra too big for the pit at the Opera House’s Joan Sutherland theatre – not to mention the massive off-stage brass ensemble scored by Wagner. OA will be hoping fans from Sydney and beyond will make the trip to Melbourne to see Scottish director McVicar’s vision for Tannhäuser. “His take on it is so extraordinary,” said Lane. “Only David’s mind could work in this brilliant way to find a pathway through this piece to make it enticing, not just for those who love Wagner, but for those who want to be in the theatre.” Leah Purcell with composer of The Drover’s Wife, George Palmer. Sam Mooy



She described initial meetings with McVicar, where he outlined his vision for Tannhäuser as “exhilarating”. In Sydney, OA is pitching the Australian premiere of Scottish Opera’s well-reviewed Magic Flute as a show for all ages in its continuing bid to capture young opera fans. Opera Australia hopes a steampunk take on Magic Flute will excite younger audiences. James Glossop “We’re trying to program family operas and build on that,” said planning and program director Ruth Thomas. “We had Hansel and Gretel earlier this year and last year we had Cendrillon [Cinderella] so we want to try and keep that [going].” Sydney’s season opens with the local premiere of perhaps the world’s best-loved opera, Puccini’s La Boheme, which has its world premiere in Melbourne in November. Sydney audiences also get a return of Simon Phillips’ production of Donizetti’s frothy comic opera The Elixir of Love, complete with ocker-ised surtitles.



Also coming to Sydney is an intriguing double-bill of one-act French works. Ravel’s L’enfant et les sortileges will feature much-loved Australian mezzo soprano Margaret Plummer. La Voix humaine, by Francis Poulenc, is a one-woman opera in which the woman makes a final phone call with her faithless lover. Leah Purcell at Opera Australia’s headquarters. Sam Mooy “You hear her side of the conversation as we as an audience have to imagine what she is hearing,” said Lane. “It is painfully intimate and so vulnerable.” Sydney’s winter season features a return of McVicar’s lush production of Faust plus Stuart Maunder’s knockabout Pirates of Penzance and a Sydney premiere of Verdi’s A Masked Ball. Melbourne also gets that city’s premiere of Ann Yee’s Turandot, the Magic Flute and Leah Purcell’s stunning The Drover’s Wife. And in a left-field programming decision, Melbourne fans will get a one-off performance of Beethoven’s 9th Symphony with the Opera Australia Chorus and Orchestra Victoria.

World.title: Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCompetition Shut down by algorithm: Small businesses suffer online nightmare David Swan August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Small businesses’ online shops are being switched off by computer algorithms with no warning or apparent human oversight, the small business ombudsman’s office says, as digital platform disputes become its biggest source of complaints. These disputes have quadrupled to 48.3 per cent of all new cases managed by the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman in the June quarter, up from 12 per cent a year earlier. Businesses built over a decade or more, with millions of dollars a year in sales running through their online accounts, can now be closed off in seconds by a system nobody has to explain, the agency warns. Jack Nekhala, inventor of the Bed Scrunchie. Sellers increasingly report their accounts being switched off entirely, rather than the isolated problems that once dominated: a hacked login, a withheld payment, a single listing pulled down. “Small businesses seeking our assistance describe how a ‘community standards’ algorithm has taken down their account without any apparent human oversight,” the ombudsman’s office told this masthead.



Last month, at least five Melbourne and Sydney queer venues were locked out of Facebook and Instagram accounts they had spent more than a decade building, with the stated reasons ranging from human exploitation to a review over alleged drugs and guns. Meta later said the accounts had been flagged in error. A suspension freezes a company’s account on such platforms, cutting sellers off from customer details and product photographs. The ombudsman’s office has urged digital platforms to provide human contacts, specific reasons and structured appeal paths before taking such action. Nekhala has lodged a complaint against Amazon with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC). AP One of the disputes has recently been taken to the competition watchdog: US inventor Jack Nekhala has lodged a complaint with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) against Amazon Commercial Services, the online giant’s local arm, after his amazon.com.au seller account was deactivated on April 11, 2025. He says there had been no Australian investigation or notice, and is asking the ACCC to establish whether anyone in Australia had assessed the decision or if it automatically followed a US block.



Nekhala invented the ‘Bed Scrunchie’, a sheet fastener business that turned over about $US6 million ($8.5 million) a year, almost all through Amazon. Trouble began in September 2024, when Amazon accepted two patent infringement complaints against the product. Nekhala’s listing was disabled for nine days and took 19 calls to Amazon support. The fix, which he eventually found in a two-year-old Reddit post rather than from Amazon, was to formally retract a complaint he says he never lodged. Then, on October 30 that year, Amazon deactivated Nekhala’s US, Canadian, Mexican and Brazilian accounts over alleged review rule breaches - the platform’s guidelines for consumer feedback, testimonials and online ratings, with nine European marketplaces following days later. Related Article Social media Queer venues locked out as Meta suspensions hit Melbourne and Sydney Weeks later, a man on LinkedIn offering Temu sales support connected Nekhala to a woman calling herself Jenna, who said she was a bedding seller with contacts inside Amazon. She was not an Amazon employee, and Nekhala says he never dealt with one directly. Over four calls, Jenna showed him internal Amazon material about his account, including enforcement classifications and investigator notes invisible to standard sellers. The records described his account block as final with an instruction not to disclose the investigation’s reason to the seller. This masthead has reviewed Nekhala’s complaint records, correspondence with Amazon and his submission to the ACCC.



Jenna offered to have an internal contact release roughly $US90,000 in frozen funds for a 20 per cent fee. Nekhala says he refused to pay, but kept the conversation going to understand the offer. “If confidential account information can leave Amazon, or if intermediaries can sell supposed influence over suspensions, complaints, reviews, listings, or frozen funds, honest Australian sellers may be competing in a marketplace where the official rules are not the only rules,” he said. Amazon said the account was permanently suspended following multiple enforcement actions for policy violations. Asked about the case by Bloomberg in June, Amazon confirmed the employee who leaked Nekhala’s information had been sacked for unrelated misconduct. A spokesman said employee involvement in fraud is very rare, and Amazon invests heavily in prevention. Nekhala says Amazon has never named the employee, provided access logs, or said whether other sellers were affected. Contacted by this masthead, Amazon confirmed that Nekhala’s account had been suspended for policy violations, without providing further details. It rejected the entrepreneur’s account that it was because it found his warranty cards, which offered customers a free accessory in exchange for registering and leaving a review, amounted to review manipulation. Nekhala says the reviews were published on his own website, weren’t linked to Amazon and never required a positive rating.



Independent sellers account for more than 60 per cent of Amazon’s global sales and thousands of Australian businesses, most of them small and medium-sized, sell in its stores, according to the online retail behemoth. Professor Jeannie Paterson of Melbourne University Law School University of Melbourne Australian sellers have several routes to support, Amazon says, including phone, email and live chats, with access to Selling Partner Support and account health specialists. Email support runs around the clock, while phone and live chat are handled between 9am and 6pm. Whether local consumer law can protect Nekhala’s contract is contested. A seller’s account being immediately deactivated due to a platform’s own risk assessment, with financial consequences and no disclosed reason, could be unfair under the Australian Consumer Law, according to University of Melbourne law professor Jeannie Paterson. “A service provider can terminate at will, but generally needs sound reasons for doing this and ideally criteria for when it will take place,” she said.



Nekhala’s Australian revenue was modest, at $US31,444 in 2023. After the shutdown, about 650 stranded bed scrunchies were handed to a distributor. The product now reaches Australian shoppers through that distributor at $99.99, up from Nekhala’s direct $79.99 price. University of Sydney academic Rob Nicholls said complaints of this kind hinge on whether they reveal a systemic problem. “If this problem has also affected a number of other, likely Australian, small businesses, then the ACCC will be concerned,” he said. The ACCC said it does not comment on complaints it receives, or on individual businesses. A spokesman said obligations under the Australian Consumer Law applied equally to every business trading in Australia, whether based here or overseas, and that whether particular conduct breached the law depended on the circumstances. “The ACCC has consistently been advocating for adequate mandatory minimum standards for digital platforms’ internal dispute resolution, and an independent external dispute resolution body for digital platform services,” a spokesman said. World.title: Four minutes of silence and an unexpected gift: Inside the ACO’s eclectic new program
World.content:
CultureMusicPerforming arts Four minutes of silence and an unexpected gift: Inside the ACO’s eclectic new program Nick Galvin August 12, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Adams, one of the world’s most influential living composers, was part way through arranging a string quartet for the Australian Chamber Orchestra when he had a sudden change of heart. “No, damn it,” the ACO’s Richard Tognetti recalls Adams deciding. “I’m going to write them a piece – a whole piece.” Richard Tognetti is still proud to be labelled an enfant terrible. Sitthixay Ditthavong The result is Gioia, a new work from the master composer created specifically for Tognetti and principal violin Satu Vanska. “Suddenly we have this extraordinary piece written for us,” says Tognetti. “We’re touring it next year in Australia and the United States. It’s the only piece he’s writing in his 80th year.”



Adams’ generous gift will be one of the highlights of a 2027 season that ranges across J. S. Bach, Part, Cage, Reich and Richard Strauss, as well as Mozart, Haydn and Schubert. Another marquee event of the ACO’s 52nd season will be an intimate performance of Bach’s transcendent St John Passion in a collaboration with award-winning Belgian vocal ensemble Vox Luminis. “The St John Passion, it’s got the whole world in it and more,” says Tognetti. “How astonishing that this dude J. S. Bach, all on his own up there in northern Germany, ends up creating music that makes him the greatest composer who ever lived.” And if the 18th-century German master were somehow to be present in the City Recital Hall to hear the ACO’s performance, what might he think? ACO principal violin Satu Vanska is one of the dedicatees of Adams’ new work. Charlie Kinross



“He’d certainly recognise it and I think he’d be delighted,” says Tognetti. “And I think he’d be surprised that his work has astral-travelled through the ages and [is] being played in this strange land of which he wasn’t even aware. Like any composer, he should be delighted his music is being kept alive.” In June the ACO will also stage its first festival, a four-day event in its Walsh Bay HQ. Entitled Currents, the event will bring together a series of eclectic programs ranging from Missy Mazzoli and Samuel Adams (son of John) to Mozart and Bach. As part of Currents, audiences will also get the chance to witness John Cage’s 4′33″, the American composer’s infamous (or revelatory, depending on your point of view) work consisting only of silence. “I did it in Maribor [Slovenia] and I tried to do it in the Adelaide Festival recently,” says Tognetti. “It’s always … a failed attempt at the exploration of nothingness. “It’s seriously confronting, on a par with trying to get a kid to meditate. You start noticing sounds in your head in the hall. Some people giggle, nervous giggles. Some people just hate it. The Brookner-loving 72-year-old classical music fan wants to kill you. And some people really find something revelatory about it.”



The 2027 season will close with the mouthwatering prospect of young soprano Masabane Cecilia Rangwanasha’s Australian debut performing Richard Strauss’ sublime Four Last Songs with an expanded ACO. Editor's pick Performing arts ‘It’s a beautiful instrument’: The young virtuoso who learnt by hugging a cello The season is classic Tognetti, by turns intriguing, challenging and revelatory. However, with him recently turning 61, I wonder whether the ACO director can still claim the badge of “enfant terrible” routinely applied to him down the years? “I think you’re born a certain age,” he says. “I’ve always sort of felt 17, so the answer is, ‘Yes, you can’. “I think the proof of the pudding is that I still get really exasperated by people if they’re not trying to get everything they possibly can from every second of every day. I’m a bit of a hard taskmaster like that.



“And with so-called classical music – and don’t we hate that expression – if a performance comes across as being in aspic, I also get exasperated.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty; CBA results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil rises on Hormuz uncertainty; CBA results ahead Stan Choe August 12, 2026 — 5:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks slipped a bit further from their records, while oil prices kept swinging on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow crude to flow freely again. The S&P 500 fell 0.3 per cent for a second modest drop since setting its all-time high on Friday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 184 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.6 per cent. Rising oil prices weighed on Wall Street. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 6am pointing to a loss of 37 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.2 per cent on Tuesday. Commonwealth Banks results are the highlight of reporting season today. The Australian dollar is trading at US70.60¢. The action was stronger in the oil market, where the price for a barrel of Brent crude briefly jumped above $US90 in the morning before falling back below $US87. It eventually settled at $US88.91, up 1.4 per cent from Monday.



Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Such erratic moves have become typical since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February, which led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and kept much of the world’s oil pent up in the Middle East. Last month alone, Brent’s price veered between $US72 and $US102 per barrel. Higher oil prices make inflation worse, and they’ve sent the average cost for a gallon of regular gasoline to $US4.01, according to AAA. That’s up from less than $US3.14 a year ago, though it’s down from last week’s nearly $US4.09. That has Wall Street’s attention focused on Wednesday, when the US government will release the latest monthly reading on inflation. Economists expect it to show inflation remains high but that it decelerated to 3.4 per cent in July from 3.5 per cent in June. That could help the Federal Reserve, whose members are notably split on whether they should be raising the country’s interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. While higher rates could help slow the increases of prices on store shelves, they would also slow the overall US economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow money. They would also undercut prices for stocks and other investments.



Traders are betting on a coin flip’s chance that the Fed will raise its main interest rate at its next meeting in September, according to data from CME Group. If it does, that would be the first increase in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates. Treasury yields have jumped since the war with Iran because of higher oil prices and worries about inflation, sending long-term mortgage rates to their highest levels in a year. The 10-year Treasury yield eased back Tuesday, falling to 4.69 per cent from 4.72 per cent late Monday. But it remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran. On Wall Street, On Holding dropped 20.3 per cent even though the Swiss sneaker company reported a better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for upcoming revenue that fell short of analysts’ expectations, while saying it does not want to slash prices to drum up more sales. Companies broadly have been blowing past analysts’ forecasts, which Wall Street loves because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term. Earnings per share for S&P 500 companies are on track to be 50 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet, and that’s a big reason US stocks have been setting records recently despite worries about expensive oil, high inflation and other challenges.



Aramark, the food company and facilities manager, rallied 8.5 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Cardinal Health added 1.3 per cent after topping analysts’ profit expectations for the spring. Related Article Opinion

The Dow Jones Industrial dropped 184.13 to 53,791.85, and the Nasdaq composite sank 159.91 to 26,445.45. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s bigger moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one?
World.content:
MoneySuper & retirementSuperannuation There are three types of super fund. Are you in the right one? Kaye Fallick August 12, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When compulsory super was introduced by the Keating Labor government in 1992, few predicted the extraordinary growth of total superannuation savings to the nearly $5 trillion it represents today. Initially, most workers joined the fund suggested by their employer. Fast-forward to 2026, and there is more complexity and a wider range of differently structured super funds from which to select. Few could have predicted the runaway success of superannuation. Simon Letch It’s important to keep abreast of your options by fully understanding the type of fund you’re in, and whether it’s time to review other options, and if so, what you need to consider. The following covers the three broad types of fund, with a note on two others. Read on to identify your fund type and what it delivers.



1. Choice funds Editor's pick Opinion

Retirement living The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong Bec Wilson Money contributor As the name suggests, a choice fund is a super fund that the member chooses. Let’s say you start your first job at the local ice-cream store. It’s compulsory for the employer to pay 12 per cent of your wage into the super fund of your choice. They may recommend one that suits your industry. But you can instruct your employer to contribute your super to any other fund you prefer. If you don’t do this, your employer can assign your savings into a MySuper option – a default fund for those who have not selected a fund or investment settings. A government initiative, MySuper has been designed as a simple, low-fee solution for those who don’t want to make active decisions about their super. Choice funds can be divided into two general categories: industry funds or retail funds.



Industry funds: As the name suggests, industry funds originally represented a band of workers doing a specific type of work, such as hospitality, transport or teaching in universities. Initially closed to other workers, most are now public offer funds, meaning anyone can join. The names of the funds have evolved to reflect this change, from industry-specific to brands such as Aware, Brighter and Australian Retirement Trust. Industry funds operate as “profit-to-member” funds and have fees set low to deliver more benefits to members. It’s possible that you could establish any one of these types of funds. It’s unlikely all would suit your personal financial situation. Retail funds: Retail funds, by comparison, were traditionally offered by banks or insurance companies. These funds were always open to any members – i.e. public offering. Some are profit-to- member, but some are “for-profit” (earnings are distributed to the company and shareholders). For many years, as industry funds gained weight in members and funds under management, retail funds showed less impressive returns. More recently, the retail funds have lowered their fees, and new entries such as Vanguard are targeting younger members.



As with the industry funds, many are also developing hybrid digital advice support. Both industry and retail super funds are regulated by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA). 2. Platform funds Also known as wrap, or master trusts, these funds offer a distinctly different member experience. While you can open a direct individual account with some, most platforms encourage members to join through a financial adviser. Platforms vary from industry and super funds because they offer a platform or administrative system that allows the saver/investor member to combine management of shares, super and other investments, including property, and receive one consolidated report. Fees for platform funds are generally higher than those for industry and retail funds, and ongoing advice consultations are usually encouraged. They are regulated by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC).



Recent research by Connexus Institute shows a major outflow over the past 12 months from choice funds to platform funds, particularly Netwealth and Hub24. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m in my 40s with $300,000 in super. Should I start an SMSF? Noel Whittaker Money columnist 3. Self-managed super funds (SMSFs) Successfully running an SMSF is not for the faint-hearted. Yes, many will suggest that they are easy to set up – but the point of super is not to start, but to finish well – i.e. to maximise your wealth at a better rate than if it was in another type of fund. Unlike choice funds, SMSFs are overseen by two regulators: the Australian Taxation Office (for compliance with super and tax laws) and ASIC for financial advice and auditors.



There are 661,000 SMSFs in Australia, covering 1.22 million members (7.2 per cent of all super fund members but 25 per cent of the pool of super savings) often held by high net worth people and business owners. One question frequently asked is: at which point does it become viable to establish an SMSF? The amount varies according to whoever is replying – but it’s generally agreed that below a $250,000 balance, the costs will outweigh the benefits. The average starting balance, according to accountancy group, H&R Block, is $400,000. Establishing a SMSF is not for the faint-hearted. Louie Douvis Apart from the fees associated with establishment of an SMSF and annual running costs, the most important requirement is that, as a trustee, you have the time, expertise and diligence to actively manage your fund. Or if you don’t, you have access to a qualified professional who can do this for you. There are two other fund types that are less common. These are public sector funds, which are available to government employees, and corporate sector funds, which are generally set up by a company for its employees only.



Which fund is right for you? While it’s possible that you could join or establish any one of these types of funds, it’s unlikely all would suit your personal financial situation. It’s important that your fund is closely aligned with your: level of savings

complexity of income, assets and investments

expectation of returns

needs and goals

preferred level or involvement, and therefore

your required level of support. Where to find out more? The Moneysmart website offers a useful summary of the features and benefits of different types of super fund. For more detail on platforms, the overview on SuperGuide is helpful. Kaye Fallick is an author, publisher, commentator and retirement income “explainer”, as well as co-creator of the Retirement Affordability Index.



Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: 'Bonkers' to fund climate disaster recovery but not prevention - local government leader
World.content:
It's "bonkers" that the government contributes to disaster recovery but not to climate adaptation to prevent damage in the first place, a local government leader says.

The Climate Change Commission on Tuesday published a progress report on how well the country is adapting to climate change, finding that delays were leaving communities exposed to future damage and costs.

It made six urgent recommendations to the government, including setting out how adaptation would be paid for.

The government should decide what it was willing to pay for itself, and then work with local councils and the private sector to find ways to fund and finance the remaining costs.

Successive governments have avoided making decisions on how to pay for adaptation, with the current government saying it would not address the issue of cost-sharing until after the election.

Local Government New Zealand regional sector chair Deon Swiggs said he largely agreed with the report's recommendations.

"It really does correctly identify that adaptation can't be delivered by local government alone."

There were already precedents out there for how adaptation costs could be shared.

"The Crown co-funds 60 percent of eligible costs after a disaster, but there's no equivalent co-funding to prevent that damage in the first place," he said.

"That's just bonkers - we should be talking about, how do we fund this stuff before it happens?

"We all know that it's cheaper to fund resilience or projects that prevent things from happening in the first place."

The National Land Transport Fund was another model that could be adapted, he said.

"That dedicates revenue, that councils apply contributions of scale to the risk, and then the rating base picks up the contribution so that you can start delivery."

The Climate Change Commission has previously pointed out that, of the $64 billion the government has spent on natural hazards since 2010, only three percent has gone to proactive measures to limit risk and damage.

A proposed law change - which the government has said is unlikely to pass before the election - would require councils to develop adaptation plans for high-risk areas at least 30 years into the future.

Councils would comply if that came into effect, but Swiggs said many of them already knew which communities were at risk.

"The reality is we can't afford to defer these conversations any further," he said.

"We've got all of this information, we've got these reports, we've got bills in [Parliament]. I think we need to work at the same time to make sure that we are talking funding."

Without that, communities would be trapped in a cycle or recovering and rebuilding.

The commission's report also recommended that the government establish funding mechanisms for iwi and Māori to adapt to climate change.

Bioeconomy Science Institute research leader Shaun Awatere. Supplied / Bioeconomy Science Institute

Bioeconomy Science Institute research leader Shaun Awatere (Ngāti Porou) said efforts to support Māori adaptation initiatives had been uneven to date.

Supporting Māori adaptation was an equity issue, but also a chance to strengthen the entire country's resilience, he said.

"During significant weather events, marae have often served as hubs for shelter, welfare support, and community coordination," he said.

Māori-led environmental initiatives were contributing to the protection and restoration of coastal areas, freshwater systems, and other resources, but were often small scale and under-resourced, Awatere said.

World.title: More tech projects struggling as govt tries to overhaul 'siloed' system
World.content:
There are major issues with two more big government IT projects, with one having to be revised after a negative rating and the other struggling to be restarted.

The latest problems come after mega-ministry MBIE wasted more than $30m on a failed biometric system that has sparked investigations in parliament.

One of the Justice Ministry's most important digital projects - to expand audio-visual links in courts - last year received a negative 'red' rating, meaning it "appears unachievable".

The ministry says it has revised the project, but is six to eight weeks away from revealing details. It was meant to have completed an early business case by this month.

The second project - to build a new system for people to access records for births, deaths and marriages - is also delayed for years.

The government chief digital officer - the watchdog of all public IT projects - has told ministers there must be more centralisation.

"Agencies' proposed digital investments continue to be siloed, duplicative and deliver little system benefit," the officer said in the latest available Treasury report, for the December 2025 quarter.

"Too many investments are overly large and span multi-years, rather than taking less risky, incremental investment and delivery approaches."

Amber-red second time round

Internal Affairs first attempted its Civil Registration project in 2024 but wrote off $23 million when that project was dumped. It confirmed this week it is still in dispute with the Australian company DWS over that.

After a second attempt, the fledgling new project received an amber/red rating in an independent 'Gateway' review in January, the department told RNZ on Tuesday.

"It received an amber/red rating, noting that the need for system replacement is compelling, but that more work is required before the IBC (indicative business case) to be ready to be submitted to government."

The department has still not decided what is needed and will not lay that out to Cabinet for approval until next year.

"The scope of any future civil registration replacement has not yet been determined. Options are being developed," it said.

Meantime, the old births-and-deaths system continues to limp along.

"While ageing, [it] is stable (although increasingly expensive to modify) and maintenance work continues to be undertaken to ensure secure, functional and legislative compliant systems."

'Continued lower confidence'

The courts and births-deaths projects are examples of chronic and persistent tech-building problems for the government, as it tries to both speed up and save on billions of dollars of demand for new digital systems.

Progress appeared to be slow.

"Investment initiatives submitted by agencies over the past six quarters point to continued lower confidence about their capacity and capability to deploy the internal expertise needed to support their projects," the government chief data steward told ministers, according to the latest available Treasury report, dated December 2025.

"Agencies are investing in modernisation, but underlying capability, standards adoption and lifecycle funding discipline remain uneven.

"Without sustained focus in these areas, the system risks increasing technical debt and cost pressures over time."

The government chief digital officer told chief executives last year to start pooling resources to build IT and stick to its standards under Cabinet's 'Back-Office Transformation' initiative.

The top IT officials and ministers had to get an early look at IT plans.

"This is critical to... the development of digital system assets that can be re-used by multiple agencies."

Revised approach

The Justice Ministry told RNZ that after it got the red rating in a Gateway review in May 2025, it revised the programme to strengthen its approach to delivering it.

Out of 10 high-risk big investments reviewed in the June 2025 quarter across public agencies, the ministry's remote participation project was the only one rated red.

"The next steps in the programme are currently under active consideration, and the ministry is not in a position to provide further detail."

The ministry and the government have expressed high hopes for several years that standardising use of AVL in courts would get many more cases heard on time and help fix the backlog. "Remote participation was invaluable during the pandemic," the ministry said on its website.

The project has now created its own backlog: The choice of tech was meant to have been finalised in early 2025. It requires a secure and reliable network and devices across many courts and tribunals.

Law changes in 2024 - and again this year -were designed to pave a path to more remote participation.

The Justice Ministry's wider digitisation programme Te Au Reka has been forecast to cost $170m.

'Largely delivered'

Internal Affairs said it was learning. "In developing options, we will be informed by the issues that arose through the phase 1 approach."

All current civil registration services remained operational, and customers continued to receive "the same service".

Civil registration had been split out from its wider $300m Te Ara Manaaki digital change programme, which closed at the end of June.

Te Ara Manaaki "largely delivered the majority of its scope", Internal Affairs told RNZ.

It received an amber-green rating on completion.

World.title: Live: Christopher Luxon calls urgent caucus meeting amid leadership speculation
World.content:
RNZ national

National Party MPs have been summoned for an "urgent in-person" caucus meeting in Wellington.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

"I am calling an urgent in-person Caucus meeting tomorrow at 9:30am in Wellington to resolve the issue."

World.title: Cost of living, water tariffs, mining on Cook Islanders' minds ahead of election
World.content:
The Cook Islands goes to the polls this week for its four-yearly general election.

Like all countries in the region, the Cooks has had its fair share of challenges due to global shocks in recent years, and there's a sense that voters are looking for some stability, particularly around the cost of living

The prime minister and leader of the Cook Islands Party, Mark Brown is in no doubt about the priority for people in this election.

He said for his party it's about consolidating the country's growth and economic recovery since reopening borders four years ago when the Cooks emerged the Covid pandemic.

"Now, that strong economic growth has allowed us to catch up, if you like, with pay increases that were halted or paused during the COVID period," he said.

"It's allowed us to increase our welfare payments, to old age pensions, child benefit, and these are all things that we're gearing up to try and meet the challenges of cost of living."

Water charges

Water utility charges are another issue in this campaign.

The leader of the Cook Islands Democratic Party, who is also the Leader of the Opposition, Tina Browne, said if elected, her party would push to remove water use tariffs for residential and agricultural users on Rarotonga.

"And we will review the present structure of [water utility] To Tatou Vai," she said.

"Of course, water infrastructure costs money. The real question is how that cost should fairly be met. I do not accept that another household bill should automatically be the first answer."

For the United Party, 'free water for all' is one of its main campaign points.

Leader of the Cook Islands United Party, Teariki Heather. RNZ Pacific / Tiana Haxton

Leader Teariki Heather said his party would remove residential water tariffs should they form government.

"Absolutely, we will revoke whatever legislation is against that for the water tariffs," he told RNZ Pacific.

His party's position is "water is a basic human right" and families shouldn't receive more bills during a cost-of-living crisis.

"On top of electricity, on top of this water tariff, the increase in cost in that, government should absorb that.

"Budget of the government is really looking at priority areas, especially this one.

"I believe that the government can assist and accommodate for the people of the Cook Islands at this particular time."

But Mark Brown pointed out infrastructure maintenance isn't free.

Leader of the Cook Islands Party, Mark Brown. RNZ Pacific / Tiana Haxton

"The question is not whether water should be free. The question is actually who's going to pay for it, because we've upgraded all of our water intakes, 10 of them, around the island in the hills of Rarotonga, and they all need to be maintained," he said.

Brown said households receive 38,000 litres free of charge per month, while churches, schools and agricultural spaces have no limit restrictions. Charges are currently only being imposed on commercial users.

"Most of these are, of course, in the tourism industry with hotels, Airbnbs, resorts, that sort of thing, and it's only fair that they contribute to the upkeep and maintenance of our water systems."

Progressive Party leader Te Tuhi Kelly said the free allocation for households is more than enough.

"If you can't manage that 38,000 litres, there's something quite wrong there because that's a lot of water, a huge amount of water, but if you go over that, I'm sorry, but you should be paying for that."

But he also thinks there are other ways government could cover water infrastructure costs.

"The water that we get from God is free; we don't pay for that. But God never put in place a delivery system for us. We have to do that ourselves. Someone has to pay for that.

"Now, whilst I'm for user pays, I think there is probably a number of other options that we can look at."

Seabed minerals

Another issue Cook Islanders are thinking about is whether the country should continue the current government's direction towards more seabed mining activity.

Teariki Heather said he will push for a referendum on seabed mining if the United Party comes to power.

While he acknowledged that exploration activities underway are potentially encouraging for generating long-term wealth in the country, he said it's so critical to protect the future health of the country, that the question of whether to progress seabed mining should be put to the people.

"But the one that we will do is put a referendum to ask the people of this country, whether this yes or no, so it's up to the people of this country [to] actually decide. That's number one that [we] will put out [to] a referendum when elected to be government."

Tina Browne agreed that a referendum is the way to go, even if science proves there would be no negative environmental impact.

"Extraction should only be considered if the evidence demonstrates that it can be done safely and in the genuine interests of the Cook Islands people. Before extraction occurs, our policy is that Cook Islanders should have the final say through a referendum."

But Te Tuhi Kelly said there is simply not enough scientific information to make a call yet.

"We're neither for, nor we're against it.

Leader of the Cook Islands Progressive Party, Te Tuhi Kelly. RNZ Pacific / Tiana Haxton

"The issue for us as a party is that the science doesn't provide me with any enthusiasm. It's young. The data is not there."

Mark Brown reiterated that the Cook Islands is only conducting exploration and research currently.

"It's important that we gain the knowledge and understanding of our deep sea before we make any decisions on whether we move to extraction or the harvesting of minerals."

When asked if the Cook Islands Party would consider a referendum, Brown said the science needs to be complete first.

"Well, it's a serious question, and again, letting people decide - first we must be able to provide the facts.

"We need to know the facts before we can make a decision, and that's why it's important that we conduct the exploration and research phase now thoroughly, in a way that ensures that, when we do ask questions of our people, our people are fully informed."

Foreign affairs

The country's relationship with New Zealand is a lingering issue too, at least in the eyes of the big parties.

This relationship came under strain after Wellington suspended some funding as a consequence of a deal that Brown's government forged with China early last year.

But Teariki Heather suggests there is a lot of work still to do to restore the healthy relationship

"New Zealand is a special one for us, and what we have discussed for this one, soon as becoming government, soon as forming the government, we make a trip, to show New Zealand how deep this relationship is."

Tina Browne also believes the relationship is all-important and needs nurturing.

"The Cook Islands should have constructive relationships with New Zealand, China, Australia, the United States, and our Pacific neighbours. We do not strengthen ourselves by unnecessarily choosing between friends."

But Mark Brown sees the situation as proof that the Cook Islands are able to "stand on their own two feet".

"We have diplomatic relations with over 70 countries around the world, including some of the biggest economies around the world. We have a foreign policy that is an independent foreign policy for the benefit of Cook Islanders.

"The fact that we can negotiate with large international countries, and the fact that we signed off on our new security and defence agreement with New Zealand on our own standing, and our own footing, on our terms, is something that people now respect for the Cook Islands and the government, the stand that we've taken."

Issues can be talked about all day, but it doesn't mean much without connecting to voters.

All of the parties realise that having a good ground game, engaging with people in their community, is the key to success.

Te Tuhi Kelly said this is particularly the case with young people

"There are a lot of kids [who] don't want to go to those political rallies because they find them boring. So what do you do if you want to get them into politics? You take politics to them.

"And what you do is you use a medium that they've grown up with, and it's a thing called social media."

The polls open at 8am Wednesday 12 August, local time (Thursday 13 August New Zealand time).

World.title: CNMI: US tax agency extends deadline for those affected by Super Typhoon Bavi
World.content:
Taxpayers across the Northern Mariana Islands affected by Super Typhoon Bavi have been given until 1 February 2027 to file a range of US federal tax returns and make payments.

The US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) announced the relief for individuals and businesses on Saipan, Tinian, and Rota following the federal disaster declaration for Bavi, which began affecting the territory on 4 July.

The IRS said deadlines that fall on or after 4 July and before 1 February 2027 may qualify for postponement.

Affected individuals and businesses will generally have until 1 February to file returns and pay taxes that were originally due during that period.

The relief also applies to people who had received a valid extension to file their 2025 individual income tax returns.

However, the IRS said tax payments associated with those 2025 returns are not covered because they were originally due on 15 April, before Bavi struck.

Quarterly payroll and certain excise tax returns normally due on 31 July and 2 November 2026, as well as 1 February 2027, are also covered by the new deadline.

Estimated income tax payments originally due on or after 21 July are also postponed until 1 February. The IRS said affected taxpayers would not face penalties for failing to make those estimated payments provided they are made by the new deadline.

The relief covers individuals living in the disaster area, and businesses - including tax-exempt organisations - whose principal place of business is there.

Some taxpayers outside the Northern Marianas may also qualify, if records they need to meet a tax deadline are located in the disaster area.

Recognised government or philanthropic relief workers assisting in the islands are also among those who may qualify.

The IRS said affected taxpayers may also claim disaster-related casualty losses on their federal income tax return, for either the year the disaster occurred or the previous year.

Individuals may be able to deduct personal property losses not covered by insurance or other reimbursements. Taxpayers claiming a Bavi-related disaster loss should include the FEMA disaster declaration number 4931-DR on their return.

Qualified disaster relief payments are generally excluded from gross income, according to the IRS.

That can include government assistance for reasonable and necessary personal, family and living expenses, as well as money for repairing or rehabilitating a home or replacing its contents.

The IRS said affected taxpayers participating in retirement plans or individual retirement arrangements may also qualify for additional relief, including certain disaster distributions that are not subject to the usual additional 10 percent early-distribution tax.
