World.title: 'Beautiful to play with' - tributes flow for former Silver Fern captain Ana Noovao
World.content:
Former Silver Fern captain Ana Noovao, who has died age 58, has been admired for the strength of her convictions and remembered as a trusted teammate by those who played with her.

The netball community is mourning the loss of Noovao, who died on the weekend after battling a long illness.

The midcourter played for New Zealand between 1989 and 1992, picking up 23 test caps.

She made her Silver Ferns debut in 1989, aged 21. When Waimarama Taumaunu retired in 1992, she was named the 15th captain of the Silver Ferns.

Former Silver Fern shooter Leoni Leaver came through the netball ranks in Auckland at the same time as Noovao.

"We both played together at College Rifles in the domestic league when it was known as the Bendon League, we were both really young. We also played in the New Zealand Young Internationals, Auckland Under 21, and then the Silver Ferns," Leaver said.

Leaver said Noovao had natural leadership qualities.

"Oh gosh, like you trusted Ana, and she was a captain that was very loyal, a captain you could just rely on her. She gave it all she had on court, she was a real feisty wing attack and beautiful to play with and you always felt safe in the team with Ana."

Ana Noovao in action during the international netball match between the Silver Ferns and Trinidad and Tobago, 1992. ©PHOTOSPORT 1992 www.photosport.nz

Noovao was a creative wing attack and Leaver said she was lucky to have been fed by her.

"I'm so blessed to have played with Ana, she was such a good wing attack and she was strong and she'd just come out for the ball and turn and release a pass in that mid-court, yeah it was amazing."

Leaver said when Noovao was made Silver Ferns' captain, it was a huge source of pride for her family and the Cook Islands community.

"She cherished her culture, where she came from, she was Cook Island through and through and did a lot for the community, and it would have been a proud moment for them to have Ana captain the Silver Ferns."

Later, Noovao played two seasons for the Cook Islands, before coaching the national side to seventh place at the 2007 World Netball Championships in Auckland.

Generations of South Auckland schoolgirls also came through her coaching sessions at local schools, and after moving to Queensland she kept playing and building the game in her new community.

"She will be remembered as being so beautiful inside and out. She was very much into the church too and I always remember she had this big cross on her wrist," Leaver said.

Silver Fern Ana Noovao in action for Auckland in 1992. www.photosport.nz

"The phone's been ringing ... we've all got on the phone and reached out to each other and the old College Rifles players, we're looking at getting together to celebrate her and just remember all the moments that we had together.

"We did so much together and back in those days, we would go back to College Rifles and bring out the guitar, you know our social life was just as good as our playing life."

Joan Hodson first met Noovao when they played together for Auckland, and were later Silver Ferns' teammates.

"We both grew up in Manurewa, in South Auckland, and I knew of her. She started off as a wing defence and I think that's why that made her such a gifted wing attack because of the pressure she used to play on them."

Hodson said Noovao had a quiet natural leadership style and stood true to her convictions.

"Ana was very religious so she made a point that she was not going to play on a Sunday, sticking to her religious beliefs but she knew that it took her away from the team and those were probably the times we got the most flogging was on a Sunday.

"She stuck to her guns in terms of her beliefs and that was part of her leadership too, she quietly went about things and definitely made up for it when she could come back and play," Hodson said.

Former Silver Fern Joan Hodson. RNZ

Former Silver Fern Teresa Tairi paid tribute to Noovao in a social media post.

"I feel extremely fortunate to have had the privilege of playing with and alongside Ana, representing both Auckland and the Auckland Cook Islands netball teams," Tairi wrote.

"Ana will always be remembered as one of the Cook Islands' finest netballers of her time - admired for her determined spirit, tenacious skills, and the quiet humility of her faith. Her contribution to netball, her strength of character, and the beautiful person she was will not be forgotten."

In a social media post, former Silver Margie Foster said Noovao was "inspiring".

World.title: All Blacks crush Sharks 54-0 in eight-try blitz
World.content:
The All Blacks have thumped the Sharks 54-0 in Durban, overcoming wet conditions to score eight tries and make it two wins from two games on their tour of South Africa.

The Sharks dominated possession and territory in the early stages of the game but it was the All Blacks who scored first in atrocious conditions in Durban with wing Fehi Fineanganofo diving over in the right corner for his first try for the national side.

Ruben Love hit the upright with the conversion but it bounced over to give the All Blacks a 7-0 lead after 20 minutes.

The tourists thought they had scored again with Damian McKenzie latching on to a Quinn Tupaea chip to slide over, but TMO replays showed he had lost the ball just before the line.

McKenzie wasn't to be denied though and scored soon after, sliding over in the right hand corner like Fineanganofo to help put the All Blacks ahead 14-0 going into halftime. McKenzie went off not long after with an injury, and was replaced by Emoni Narawa.

Damian McKenzie scores in wet conditions in Durban. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

The All Blacks thought they had struck first in the second half when hooker Asafo Aumua barged his way over from close range, but the try was disallowed by the TMO who couldn't see the ball clearly grounded over the line.

However, the tourists would score a couple of phases later with left wing Caleb Clarke dotting down after an easy run to the line following an overlap. Love nailed the sideline conversion to increase the All Blacks lead to 21-0.

Fineanganofo then grabbed his second try of the match after some good play from Love and Clarke and Love continued his perfect record off the kicking tee to put the All Blacks ahead 28-0 with 25 minutes to go.

Fehi Fineanganofo scores a try for the All Blacks. Samuel Shivambu/BackpagePix

Hooker Bradley Slater and prop Siale Lauaki came off the bench to make their All Blacks debuts, as the visitors replaced their entire front row, before midfielder Jordie Barrett scored a great team try where the All Blacks handling skills in the wet were on display.

Love kicked the extras to give the All Blacks a 35-0 lead and then there was a roar from the crowd as former All Blacks centurion Ma'a Nonu came on for the Sharks as a replacement at 44 years old.

The All Blacks were starting to run rampant and halfback Kyle Preston was the next to score after another great piece of interplay between the New Zealand backs, which was sparked by a break from Quinn Tupaea..

Love kicked his sixth straight conversion to put the All Blacks ahead 42-0 and it wasn't long before the All Blacks had their seventh try, with replacement back Timoci Tavatavanawai scoring in the left corner with 10 minutes remaining to extend their lead to 47-0. Love missed the sideline conversion this time to spoil his perfect record, but it was still an impressive night with the boot for the first-five.

Ruben Love kicked well against the Sharks. Ron Gaunt/www.photosport.nz

Lock Sam Darry got his name on the scoreboard with the All Blacks eighth try of the game, using his long arms to reach out and slam the ball down over the tryline and help the tourists push out to a 54-0 lead with five minutes to go and that's how the score would remain, as the All Blacks made it two wins from two games on their tour of South Africa.

'Awesome steps forward' - captain

It was an "awesome game to be a part of," captain Luke Jacobson said in a sideline interview afterwards.

"I think we broke them down well in the first half and we got the fruits of that in the second half and we came away with a good win.

"Against the Stormers (the first game) we weren't where we wanted to be with our set piece around our maul and our scrum, we took awesome steps forward there this week.

"Out there in these wet conditions it's about skill execution and probably didn't start that well there but we started executing really well and we ended up getting points from it.

"It's about trusting your skill sets, trusting your mate, being patient and not being too eager."

The All Blacks next play the Bulls in Pretoria on Sunday morning (NZT).

World.title: Women coaches have almost tripled, but 'misogynistic and abusive' behaviour remains
World.content:
If you asked generative AI to create an image of a sports coach, it would likely serve up a middle-aged white man.

And while rooted in stereotypes, it would not necessarily be inaccurate.

The picture is slowly changing in some sports, although not substantial enough yet to disturb the algorithm.

The Australian Institute of Sport found the number of female head coaches in funded sports has nearly tripled since starting its Women in High Performance Coaching project in 2021.

The number now sits at more than 25 per cent, but AIS Director Matti Clements told ABC Sport that is still not good enough.

"Maybe we've had a history where we've just had male coaches coaching our best athletes," she said.

"We want to make sure the right people are coaching our athletes at the right time, female or male coaches."

AIS director Matti Clements says many female coaches still face key barriers. (ABC News: Peter Healy)

The AIS report found many women coaches have experienced bad behaviour, which was "in some cases appalling, misogynistic and abusive," as well as challenges managing careers alongside having a family, and difficulties even getting a foot in the door, let alone climbing the ladder.

It highlighted the need for leaders within the sporting sector to drive cultural change to address the barriers.

"As a system, we've had a real focus in the last couple of years of wellbeing being fundamental to high performance sport in this country," Clements said.

"If you look at wellbeing as a sustainable high-performance lever, that will encourage all different types of people to stay in our system, female coaches included.

"Perhaps historically, high-performance sport in this country has not been as welcoming for female coaches as it has been for male coaches."

Clements pointed out some of the strategies which have helped deliver positive results over the past four years include visibility of high profile coaches, having conversations at the highest levels, re-evaluating recruitment practices, and targeted development.

Sauvage leading the way

Louise Sauvage is one of Australia's most decorated Paralympians, and since retiring in 2004, has established herself as a leading coach in para wheelchair track and road racing.

She has noticed an evolution over the past 20 years.

Louise Sauvage has been an elite coach for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

"It's been really good to see that infrastructure and also the investment into women's coaching," she told ABC Sport.

"Our athletes are almost 50-50 male, female, so to have that balance is perfect.

"And I think women bring something a little different to the male coaches as well. So I think it's important that we encourage them to continue on in those roles and to show the identity and what we can bring as female coaches."

Sauvage is also one of very few elite coaches with disability across the Australian sporting landscape, and acknowledged it has not always been an easy path for her.

"I think some of the barriers were definitely identifying what you could or couldn't do or how the workarounds would work," she said.

"And also talking with your national sporting organisation and how you can get past them or what help you might need and then you can just be as effective as any other coach.

"I think it's about communication more than anything and not just looking at something [and saying] 'oh, I can't do that.'

"[You should ask] how can you do it? How can we make it work for you so that you can progress as a coach?"

She added having coaches with shared lived experiences was a valuable asset for athletes.

"They already know that I know how they're feeling or what they need because I've been there and I've done that," she said.

"But things evolve all the time, so I need to keep learning as well. But I really do think a lot of the athletes do appreciate that the understanding is already there."

The professional picture

The AIS report focused on sports it funds, largely rooted in the Olympic and Paralympic arena, but many of the issues raised prevail in the professional codes too.

Four of the 18 of AFLW head coaches are women, one of 12 in the NRLW, one of 11 in the A-League Women and two of eight in the WBBL (last season).

The WNBL is close to parity with four of the nine coaches women, and as the country's number one female participation sport, five of Super Netball's eight coaches were female last season.

Like the dearth of disabled coaches, there are also very few First Nations, or culturally diverse head coaches, across men's and women's sports.

Clements said diversity in coaching simply makes sense.

"The sports are seeing the value of it in terms of performance outcomes. So this is not just a nice to have, we're doing it because it feels good," she said.

"It absolutely is a competitive advantage and that's what's going to engage our sports to continue to focus on this because we want to have the best games ever in Brisbane and in order to do that we have to make sure we've got the best people coaching."

World.title: Cats confirm Kolodjashnij unavailable to play amid concussion waiver saga
World.content:
The player at the centre of a concussion waiver controversy, Geelong's Jake Kolodjashnij, will not play this weekend as the club prepares to find out whether it will face sanctions.

It emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with a player, who had had a history of concussions.

Kolodjashnij went public confirming he was the player involved.

The waiver has since been removed from his contract.

"Geelong Cats defender Jake Kolodjashnij will be unavailable for selection at AFL or VFL level this weekend," the club said a statement late on Tuesday.

"The care and wellbeing of Jake remains the club's priority, and the club will continue to support him and his family through this period."

The Cats had until the end of Tuesday to respond to the "please explain" from the AFL over the concussion waiver that Kolodjashnij signed but which was never seen by the AFL or the AFLPA.

Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's please explain as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board had held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Media reports on Tuesday said that the AFL Commission had hired independent legal counsel to help determine whether the Cats should face sanctions over the issue.

The 31-year-old Kolodjashnij was drafted by the club in 2013 and he has played 209 games for Geelong.

He last played at AFL level for the Cats against GWS a month ago.

His twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, was forced to retire in 2020 due to concussion issues.

World.title: Veteran Manly prop Nathan Brown outlines NRL exit plan
World.content:
Manly prop Nathan Brown has revealed he decided at the start of the season this would be his last in the NRL, as the veteran forward eyes a move to the Super League.

Off contract at the end of 2026, Brown has confirmed he will finish up at Manly this year as the Sea Eagles begin a changing of the guard in the forward pack.

Brown's final month at Manly will take on even more importance on Friday night, after he was called in to start for the first time in two years against the Dolphins amid the Sea Eagles' forwards shortage.

The 33-year-old is still hoping to exit the NRL in a finals series, with Manly likely needing to win their last four games to return to the top eight.

Munster free to play Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster avoids suspension after the NRL match review committee downgrades his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

"I just knew it was my time to call it quits in the NRL … I made my debut in 2013, so it's my 14th year. When your time's up, your time is up," Brown told AAP.

"The last thing I wanted to do was sit on the fence with whether I want to stay or go overseas.

"It's just made everything a lot easier to go all in this year and enjoy every moment, every training session and every game."

Brown was regarded as one of the most aggressive forwards in the game when he debuted at Wests Tigers in 2013, as well as during a two-year stint at South Sydney.

Nathan Brown played six seasons at the Eels, making his Origin debut while at the club. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yeung)

He came into his own at Parramatta, playing two State of Origins for NSW in 2020 and the 2022 grand final for the Eels before reviving his career with a train-and-trial deal at Manly in 2024.

"I find it funny [looking back at old footage)]" said Brown, who is on track to reach 200 games this month.

"When I started, I was a lot bigger. I wasn't really that fit. I was a bit overweight for my size and my position. And I had a different attitude back then.

"But at the same time, you learn a lot from it. You feel grateful that you had to go through those things."

Brown's NRL retirement comes with fellow veteran Manly prop Siua Taukeiaho off contract after breaking his leg in two places in May.

The Sea Eagles have signed props Davvy Moale and Toni Mataele for next year, while Kayliss Fatialofa will arrive as a highly-heralded second rower.

Teenage prop Simi Laiafi has also shown promise starting this year alongside Taniela Paseka, and looms as a long-term prospect.

Brown said he was proud of the impact he was able to have off the bench this year, still hitting the line with gusto.

"You don't want to be finishing by just clutching at the straws and hanging on by a thread," he said.

"I feel like I can probably still physically play another year in the NRL. But in the mental side of things, I'm just ready."

Manly expect to be without prop Paseka for at least a fortnight after he injured his knee against Melbourne last week, in a seismic blow to their finals chances.

Ethan Bullemor (concussion) remains sidelined, while Kobe Hetherington (biceps) last week joined Taukeiaho in being out for the season.

Second-rower Ben Trbojevic (concussion) is also still out, while his superstar brother Tom has been kept on ice for another week in his return from a hamstring injury.

World.title: Slater still firing at 54 at Tahiti Pro, eliminating Medina
World.content:
Kelly Slater has advanced to the third round of the Tahiti Pro after the 54-year-old American overcame Brazil's Gabriel Medina and ​some heavy wipeouts at the 2024 Paris Olympics venue of Teahupo'o.

Slater's emotional Margaret River exit Surfing legend Kelly Slater holds back tears as his career effectively ends at Western Australia's Margaret River Pro, although the 11-time world champion is hoping for one last wildcard in Fiji.

Slater, who recently underwent hip surgery, retired from full-time competition in 2024 and welcomed a third child earlier this year ​but showed he had ‌lost none of his competitive edge against three-times world champion Medina.

In dangerous, challenging waves, Slater got smashed on his first attempt and was hit even harder on ‌his second wave, breaking his board in two.

But the Floridian recovered ⁠and threaded a long, deep tube that scored a 9.73 ‌out of 10 to take ​the lead.

He ‌then backed it up with another excellent score to advance over Medina, who beat Slater in an epic final at the same venue in 2014.

"I don't know if I'll ever have another heat with him, and ​he ‌got me last time," said Slater, who dominated the first day of competition.

He said he had been motivated by criticism of the ⁠decision to award him a wildcard ‌to compete.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"You see those comments, ‌a lot of people doubting me or saying [the opportunity] should have gone to ‌a local wildcard," he said. "Even after all this time, I have something to prove."

Slater finished with an excellent two-wave ‌total ​of 19.06 out of ⁠20 to set up a third-round meeting with reigning champion Jack Robinson of Australia, who was pushed hard by countryman Callum Robson in round two.

California's Griffin Colapinto, who was born six years after ⁠Slater won the first of his 11 world titles, was the only man to better Slater's ‌performance in ‌the second round, racking up a perfect 10-point ride ​on his way to a season-high heat total of 19.6 out of 20.

World.title: Vine time: Matildas hero seals A-League Women return
World.content:
Cortnee Vine has returned to A-League Women with champions Melbourne City in a move that could help the Matildas' penalty shootout hero push for a second Women's World Cup berth.

Elsewhere, Matildas great and Brisbane captain Tameka Yallop has joined Wellington in a huge recruiting coup for the grand finalists.

Vine, 28, starred for Sydney FC as an explosive and tricky winger, winning three premierships and two championships.

Vine catapulted to stardom when she scored the winning spot-kick in the Matildas' famous penalty shootout against France that secured a maiden Women's World Cup semi-final berth in 2023.

The winger joined North Carolina Courage in 2024 but made just 23 appearances in two years, scoring twice, while also taking time away from football to prioritise her mental health.

With golden boot winner Holly McNamara leaving City for Super League club Everton, Vine is instantly the club's biggest name.

"I'm really excited to be coming home and joining Melbourne City," Vine said in a statement.

"I've watched what City has achieved over the last few seasons and the standards this group continues to set, so the opportunity to come into that environment and be part of a team competing for trophies was really exciting to me.

"My time in the NWSL has helped me grow both as a player and a person, and I'm looking forward to bringing those experiences back to Australia."

Vine will have the opportunity to impress and push for three trophies across the ALW and the Women's Asian Champions League.

Tameka Yallop has left Brisbane Roar after 158 games and 66 goals in various stints since 2008. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Attacking midfielder Yallop looms as the missing piece for Bev Priestman's Phoenix.

Yallop's wife Kirsty Yallop is a former New Zealand international and the move allows the couple and their two young daughters to be closer to family.

The 35-year-old, who missed this year's Asian Cup through injury, can also press her Women's World Cup case with the ambitious Phoenix.

Bev Priestman took Wellington Phoenix to the grand final in her first season at the helm. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"I'm chasing that trophy and so is Wellington, so we're aligned," Yallop said.

"Getting the opportunity to work under Bev was a massive drawcard, not to mention the facilities at NZCIS. They're second to none.

"It's a high performance environment in Wellington and that's something that I love being a part of.

"And the Phoenix have shown they're dedicated to their women's program. That was a major pull for me too."

Loading Instagram content

Brisbane is retiring the former Julie Dolan Medallist's number 13 jersey — the first time the club has done so for a men's or women's player.

Yallop, who has attended four World Cups and three Olympics and played overseas in several top leagues, spent the majority of her decorated A-League Women career at the Roar, bar a one-season stint at City in 2018-19.

An inaugural Queensland Roar player at the age of 17 in 2008, Yallop won three premierships at Brisbane and scored in two grand final wins.

Yallop scored 66 goals in 158 games in three separate stints at the Roar.

The new season is due to start on Friday October 16.

World.title: 'Never forgotten where he's from': Outback community pride for Crows legend
World.content:
Taylor Walker will go down in history as an AFL legend but when all is said and done, the boy from the bush wants to return home and attempt to win a premiership in the town that made him.

Walker announced his retirement from the Adelaide Crows Football Club on Monday after 19 seasons playing for the AFL club.

The 36-year-old's playing career started in the outback New South Wales community of Broken Hill, located just over the South Australian border.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year," he said in his retirement announcement speech.

Jayden Kelly is one of those mates and says he is holding Walker to that promise.

Jayden Kelly played junior footy with Walker, and is hopeful he'll come back to Broken Hill and play. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

"He has mentioned it once or twice that he would love to [come back]. So there's myself and a couple of his close mates that are just hanging on and still playing local footy back here," he said.

Walker is no stranger to a winning a flag with the North Broken Hill Football Club.

As a self-proclaimed "skinny kid from Broken Hill", the then 17-year-old helped the Bulldogs to premiership glory in 2007.

Taylor Walker (left) was instrumental in the 2007 grand final, when the North Broken Hill Bulldogs won. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

Broken Hill inspiration

But while Taylor Walker will undoubtably be remembered for his on-field contributions for the Crows, the legacy he leaves in Broken Hill is just as significant.

Kelly said Walker's career had shown young people in the town what could be possible.

"He's really put us on the map," he said.

"He's shown young kids in Broken Hill, if they put their mind to it and by working hard, what they can achieve."

Kelly, who played junior football alongside Walker, said he remembered feeling it was "unreal" to see a boy from Broken Hill picked when he was drafted .

"Being able to go and live out a childhood dream; he supported the crows growing up and had all the Tony Modra posters all over his wall," he said.

"He loved everything Crows and when he got the phone call that they were interested ... he was over the moon."

Taylor Walker plays alongside fellow Crow and Broken Hill export Isaac Cumming. (Supplied: AFC Media)

Wayne Walker is Taylor Walker's dad who proudly remains living in the outback town.



He said he had most admired his son's relationship with his family, the Adelaide Crows and club supporters.

"He's always never forgotten where he come from. His mates are so dear to him, it's not funny, they keep him grounded," he said.

"That's probably one thing he has been, he's been very grounded during the whole 19 years."

Walker's friends and family say he's never forgotten where he came from. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

It is a sentiment Walker's friend, Jayden Kelly agreed with.

"He's had so many ups and downs, the resilience he has shown, and he's never forgotten where he's come from," he said.

"He's so loyal to the people around him, to his family, and to the town that he grew up in.

World.title: Aussie open water swim queen Johnson triumphs at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's world champion Moesha Johnson has continued her season of complete dominance in open water swimming, winning the Pan Pacific Championships 10-kilometre title off Long Beach, California.

Racing on the same waterfront expected to be used for the 2028 Olympics, 28-year-old Johnson grabbed the lead on the second of six laps and won comfortably in one hour 55 minutes and 33 seconds on Tuesday (AEST).

She finished more than 26 seconds clear of silver medallist Airi Ebina of Japan, with Ichika Kajimoto (Japan) third and fellow Australian Jacqueline Davison-McGovern fifth in the 23-strong field.

"I really wanted to win going into the race today, and it's a strong group of girls, they're really fit and everyone's in really good shape," Johnson said after the race.

World.title: 'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
World.content:
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.

The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.

The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.

On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.

The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.

Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.

PTPA says 'evidence is clear'

The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.

'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner pulls out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.

The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.

The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.

The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.

"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."

Schedule the players' choice

The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.

Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.

It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.

It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

Reuters

Tech.title: ChatGPT and Gemini both just passed 1 billion users
Tech.content:
For the 14th time, a Google product has hit 1 billion users. Google CEO Sundar Pichai posted on X that a billion people are using Gemini every month, and that Gemini is Google’s fastest-growing product ever.

A billion users is a huge milestone, but Google isn’t the first AI app to hit it. OpenAI’s ChatGPT hit the mark a few weeks ago, though the company buried the announcement that “more than 1 billion people are putting ChatGPT to work” in an otherwise anodyne blog post about how people use AI. External data suggested ChatGPT crossed 1 billion users as early as this June, but OpenAI hadn’t announced anything until that post on August 6th. OpenAI spokesperson Lindsay McCallum says ChatGPT crossed 1 billion monthly users some time ago, and hit a billion a week in July.

The metrics, and the growth they represent, are somewhat complicated here. OpenAI said that ChatGPT had 900 million weekly active users in February of this year, and reaching 1 billion five months later represents a significant slowdown in growth for ChatGPT, which was for years touted as the fastest-growing software ever. McCallum declined to say how many monthly users ChatGPT has.

Google, meanwhile, announced in February that Gemini had 750 million monthly users, before reporting 950 million in late July on its earnings call, and Google spokesperson Alex Joseph says it reached 1 billion last week before announcing it today. (Claude appears to be growing fast, but Anthropic doesn’t disclose its user data, and estimates put its user numbers in the tens of millions.) There’s no easy way to compare weekly and monthly users, of course, but the simplest read is that ChatGPT is the larger of the platforms but Gemini may be the faster growing.

These Google numbers, by the way, all appear to refer directly to the Gemini app itself, which would mean all the places Google has shoved Gemini into its other products don’t count. The Gemini that comes preinstalled on Android phones seemingly does, though, which is a huge win for Google — Gemini chief Josh Woodward posted that Gemini has more than 100 million active users on iOS, which would mean by extension that the vast majority of Gemini users are also Android users. You can see why OpenAI is so interested in building its own hardware.

The AI race in general has tightened significantly this year. Anthropic’s Claude Code became a phenomenon and forced OpenAI to catch up with Codex, while Google began integrating Gemini into seemingly every surface of its products. The companies’ models have consistently leapfrogged each other, and they’re all suddenly in a race with models coming out of China. But for a long time, ChatGPT was the de facto brand for AI chatbots, and while it’s still seemingly the most popular and well known of its kind, its once commanding lead appears to have largely evaporated. The race to a billion users is over — now these companies have to race to find things for those users to do, and ways to make money in the process.

Tech.title: Another OpenAI executive takes off
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Brad Lightcap, OpenAI’s special projects lead and the company’s former COO, announced his departure after an eight-year stint at the AI lab. In an internal memo he later posted to X, Lightcap told colleagues he’d be starting “something new.”

“Over the last few months, I’ve been focused on the next horizon and what would stand in the way of mission success,” Lightcap wrote. “I believe there are a few important new things the world will need to get right as we enter this next period. I … am excited to help you all advance the mission from a different vantage point.” He added that he’d still be around for the next few weeks.

Lightcap’s role has changed a lot over the past year and a half. In March 2025, his role as COO expanded to include overseeing OpenAI’s “business and day-to-day operations,” heading up global deployment and “focusing on business strategy, key partnerships, infrastructure, and operational excellence to maximize the impact of our research.” Then in January 2026, Lightcap took a step back from leading the company’s enterprise push as far as product and engineering but stayed in charge of commercial functions. (Embattled AI executive Barret Zoph took over enterprise before departing about five months later.) In April, Lightcap officially stepped down from his COO role, transitioning into a new one leading the team’s “special projects” and reporting to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Denise Dresser, the company’s CRO, took over a significant portion of his former role.

It’s not the only high-profile departure from OpenAI’s executive team in recent months: OpenAI’s AGI chief, Fidji Simo, officially departed her role in July after a stint on medical leave, and in April, CMO Kate Rouch also stepped down for health reasons. There’s also been a significant amount of company reorganizing and C-suite changes, with company president Greg Brockman taking control of the product side of things, and the company vowing to cut out “side quests” in favor of key revenue drivers as it prepares to go public over the coming year.

“It always amazes me how quickly the world has adopted our tools and rallied behind our mission,” Lightcap wrote. “I hope we will continue to earn their trust.”

Tech.title: Google’s upcoming Pixel phones are for the fans, even if its launch event isn’t
Tech.content:
Last year’s Made by Google event for the Pixel 10 resembled a late night talk show, complete with Jimmy Fallon as host, and it aired an hour after the phones were revealed. Spec dives and executive appearances were replaced with celebrity cameos and awkward skits, to the confusion of many diehard Pixel fans. But it served its purpose in reaching a broader audience: Last year’s stream racked up 8.4 million viewers on YouTube; the launch the year before only managed 1.4 million.

This year, Google has only escalated matters. For tomorrow evening’s livestream, Fallon has been replaced by Trevor Noah, who will lead a “stacked” lineup of celebrities including basketball star Stephen Curry, podcaster Alex Cooper, and DJ Peggy Gou. What the event won’t have is many surprises. While the launch event kicks off at 6PM ET, the Google Store’s preorder countdown is set to end eight hours earlier, presumably when the phones will be revealed in full.

By the time Google’s stream starts, its most avid fans will know exactly what’s coming. Then again, for the most part, they already do. In a world where almost every spec leaks ahead of time, it makes sense that Google’s celeb-centric launch event won’t be targeted at Pixel power users.

Google’s been one of the most adaptive companies when it comes to the modern proliferation of phone leaks. Last year it took the unusual step of simply revealing the Pixel 10 design in full almost a month ahead of the launch. This year it’s only showed glimpses of the Pixel 11 series, but in the process has revealed something that should excite most power users more than the launch itself: a notification light.

The light is built into the camera island of the Pixel 11 Pro (though perhaps not the regular model), where the flash normally is, suggesting that it serves as the flash and flashlight too. It’s a small feature, but a surprisingly big part of Google’s smartphone heritage. The majority of Google’s Nexus phones included hardware notification LEDs, and Google was one of the last manufacturers to drop the feature, which saw a brief resurgence in 2017’s Pixel 2 before Google binned it off again — we thought for good. The RGB lights could be used to show the phone’s charging status, flash when notifications come in, and activate in different colors. Open-source Android skins like CyanogenMod and apps like Light Flow gave even more flexibility, letting users set specific colors and blink rates for specific apps or contacts.

Notification LEDs went out of fashion about the same time that the always-on display came in. Who needs a little light when you can have the actual notifications on the screen at all times? Some Android phones instead include the option to have the edges of the display flash a certain color when notifications come in, which can even be visible when the phone is face down, depending on the design, but dedicated lights have been few and far between.

Nothing’s Phone 2 made a statement out of its Glyph Lights. Photo by Allison Johnson / The Verge

The most prominent recent examples have all come from Nothing, which has elevated the LED into an art form. Ever since 2022’s Nothing Phone 1, it’s incorporated complex light arrays and dot-matrix displays into the back of its phones, allowing not just quick flashes but complex, customizable patterns or icons that can vary by contact or app. There’s only one other recent phone I can think of to feature a dedicated LED, though in the case of the Trump phone, it felt like proof of its dated, recycled design rather than a forward-thinking feature.

The small light shown in the camera bar of the 11 Pro is more subtle than most of Nothing’s designs, though seemingly more colorful. Google hasn’t said what the light can do, though since the pulsing, multicolored animation resembles some of the Gemini design language, it seems a smart guess that it relates to Google’s AI assistant. Leaks suggest it may light up when you talk to the chatbot or receive calls from certain contacts, though I hope Google has more in mind for it than that, with the same customizability by app and by contact that Nothing phones support. The cruelest trick of all would be to bring back the notification light and then not have it light up for notifications.

Perhaps it’s odd that on the eve of Google’s flagship phone launch I’m most excited about the apparent resurrection of a feature Google sent to the graveyard nine years ago. I presume the new Pixel phones will also be interesting in other ways, with the usual chipset bumps, camera upgrades, and design language tweaks.

But as the company pushes into entirely new ways of launching its phones to entirely new audiences, there’s a charm in it giving its oldest fans what they want when it comes to the hardware itself. Somehow I doubt it’s going to dig any further and reveal a Pixel 11 with a 3.5mm headphone jack, microSD card slot, or replaceable battery, but at least we can dream.

Tech.title: Made by Google 2026: all the Pixel news and announcements

Comedian Trevor Noah will host this year’s show, featuring notable guests like NBA star Stephen Curry, podcaster Alex Cooper, Indian cricketer Shubman Gill, and Japanese actress Ayami Nakajo.
